title: Coffee prices hit fresh highs as weather wreaks havoc on c rops in Brazil and Vietnam, with Australian roasters under the pump:   This year droughts are pushing coffee prices to record highs, but climate change means it's unlikely we'll ever see a return to the $3 flat white.
author: Jasper, Clint
full_text:
The cost of importing coffee beans into Australia has never been more expensive, & there are few signs these record prices will ease anytime soon.
While wages, rents & operational costs account for the vast majority of what you pay for a coffee, inclement weather in coffee-producing regions overseas is also putting upward pressure on prices of everything from a servo cuppa to a specialty flat white.
And with global demand for coffee on track to outstrip supply within two decades, the industry is facing a tough financial grind.
Last week, Nestle Global CFO Anna Manz told investors rising input costs would affect margins in the coming six months.
"Coffee & cocoa are [contributing] definite upward pressure but we've got benefit elsewhere," Ms Marz said.
And one of the world's largest coffee roasters, Lavazza, recently told Bloomberg News higher bean prices, shipping costs & a stronger US dollar had added 800 million euros ($1.3 billion) to the Italian company's costs in the past two years.
While it doesn't tell the whole story, recent analysis from Sydney-based Pablo & Rusty's Coffee Roasters shows the coffee itself accounts for about 12 per cent of the price of your average small takeaway flat white.
The company's CEO, Abdullah Ramay, said the escalating prices were initially something the company's buyers thought might blow over in three to six months.
"I think that view has changed … both on the coffee front, which we don't see resolving anytime soon, & also on the Australian dollar front," he said.
So what's behind the rise in price?
The world's biggest coffee-producing regions have both been hit at once
Arabica coffee beans grow best when the temperature stays between 18 & 22C, & there's about 1,200mm of rain distributed throughout the year, according to Brazilian agronomist Jonas Leme Ferraresso.
In Brazil, where the vast majority of the world's arabica coffee beans are produced, growers are harvesting a second drought- & heatwave-plagued crop.
This season, Brazil's arabica crops have sweltered through temperatures in the high 20s, & haven't received enough rain to reach optimal yields.
"For arabica, which is more sensitive to high temperatures, when the temperature exceeds 33C, the plant's photosynthetic rate approaches 0 per cent, meaning there is no adequate development of leaves, seeds & roots," Mr Ferraresso said.
"[From August last year to now] on various days & times, almost all arabica regions experienced this problem, especially during the period of development & expansion of coffee beans."
Arabica prices climbed to just under $8.50/kg at the start of July.
[Arabica prices]
Of Brazilian coffee growers, 72 per cent are small-hold farmers on around 20 hectares of land, according to a 2017 agricultural census taken by the Brazilian Institute of Statistics & Geography.
Higher prices have helped most stay profitable, even though yields are down, Mr Ferraresso said.
"Coffee prices on the international markets, remaining at current levels, & with our exchange rate, is a profitable business," he said.
"The biggest problem today is related to labour, which is scarce & expensive, & with each agricultural year, the situation worsens."
At the same time in Vietnam, where robusta coffee is the dominant crop, production & exports have been slashed as the country endures one of the worst droughts on record.
Robusta is the main variety used for instant coffee, & the preferred bean for larger global producers, many of which have taken their significant buying power into the arabica market, & maintained the upward pressure on prices there.
The world's third-largest producer, Colombia, will also harvest a smaller crop this season, according to USDA estimates.
Robusta beans are now at record highs, nearly double where they were a year ago.
[Robusta prices] Consumers will taste the difference in their cup
Despite the difficult season, arabica production in Brazil is still expected to lift slightly in 2024/25, & world-ending stocks (the measure that refers to everything left over after the year's consumption) are tipped to rise slightly.
[Ending stocks]
But even with the expected recovery in Brazilian coffee volumes, Australian importers expect quality to drop.
"What they're seeing at the moment, which will filter down to consumer level, is they have a very low screen size, because they've had such poor weather," FTA Coffee general manager David McKennariey said.
Mr McKennariey said arabica had been trading well above prices seen at any point over the past five years, putting financial pressure on local roasters.
"It has always been the cheapest arabica as a generalisation, & as coffee prices have gone up, roasters have pivoted away from some of the more expensive origins to Brazil," he said.
"It has more than doubled compared to what it has been over the past a couple of years."
At the Blacklist Coffee Roasters' warehouse in south-eastern Perth, production manager Ernest Ho is paying "80 to 90 per cent" more for green beans this year than he was in 2021.
In the past year alone, prices lifted 16 per cent.
The company, which sells its roasted beans all over Australia, relies on backup suppliers & trains its roasting team to produce consistent results with multiple blends to ensure it is not over-exposed to price swings in any particular region.
"There are different regions around the world which can produce similar-tasting profile coffees, obviously a different cost," Mr Ho said.
"At the end of the day, what matters to our consumers is what's in the cup of coffee.
"We also try & relay the message that, because coffee is a natural product, as much as we try & lock in a particular taste profile for coffee, there's always going to be some variations involved."
The rise in home brewing changed the game too
A combination of pandemic-era restrictions on hospitality venues, followed by a cost-of-living crisis, has driven many Australians to become their own baristas at home.
Mr Ho can see that playing out through Blacklist's online sales to individuals, which grew 80 per cent per year in 2020/21 & 2021/22.
"This last two fiscal years, we're seeing a slowdown of the growth in terms of online," he said.
"But we are generally seeing a lot more consumers buying bags of coffee … then brewing that at home."
Mr McKennariey said supermarket coffee bean brands, particularly at Aldi, had proven particularly popular with at-home coffee makers.
"Lots of Australian households that have [bean-to-cup] espresso machines … are purchasing from supermarkets," he said.
"Luxio, in the Aldi supermarket, instead of that being manufactured in Germany & shipped out, they roast it locally in Melbourne.
"They're offering single origins. The quality of that coffee, personally, I think is comparable to some of the better quality cafes from maybe 10 years ago."
In any case, expect to start paying more for coffee
The land available with the right conditions to cultivate coffee is expected to shrink because of climate change, according to researchers at Zurich University.
Meanwhile, demand for coffee keeps expanding, with current projections from World Coffee Research estimating a 35 million bag shortfall in robusta alone.
A greater number of people making coffee at home is a positive sign for an industry that will be charging higher prices for coffee in the future, according to Mr Ramay.
Comparing it to the willingness of enthusiastic home cooks to spend more on a meal at a restaurant, Mr Ramay said Australians needed to start getting used to paying more for coffee.
"Cafe prices need to move, & hopefully people understand why they're moving," he said.
"Especially for independent cafes — larger chains can use coffee as a loss leader, or as a break-even exercise because it gets people in the door & they can spend on other things.
"But [for smaller cafes] a day comes when your back's against the wall. So it's like 'OK, my choice is go out of business or raise prices'."

title: Woodside's slow going on clean energy spend
author: Angela Macdonald-Smith
full_text:
Woodside Energy boss Meg O'Neill has blamed customer reluctance to pay a premium for higher-cost green energy products for the slow progress towards the oil and gas producer's targeted $US5 billion ($7.8 billion) spend on "new energy" this decade.
The Perth-based company last month signalled a delay to its flagship green energy project, the H2OK liquid hydrogen venture in Oklahoma. It cited the timing of regulatory decisions related to production tax credit criteria under the Biden administration's Inflation Reduction Act, and slow progress signing customers.
Ms O'Neill told investors yesterday that Woodside is still holding to the $US5 billion spending target for new energy by 2030 that it announced two years ago, but acknowledged progress had been "modest". Potential projects also include low-carbon ammonia, solar power and carbon capture.
The pace of investment in clean energy compares with up to $US24.4 billion budgeted for three large-scale oil and gas projects in Western Australia, Mexico and Senegal, which appear to fly in the face of its net-zero commitment for direct emissions by 2050. It fuelled renewed criticism from activist shareholder group the Australasian Centre for Corporate Responsibility that Woodside is not serious about its carbon reduction strategy.
But Ms O'Neill said Woodside had always envisaged a gradual ramp-up in spending on new energy as the market took shape.
"We signalled that the spend was going to ramp up as we go through the 2020s," she said after an investor briefing in Sydney. "Customers are going to have to think about how they use a different energy product than they are used to using.
"The costs right now are higher than the products they are using today."
Shares in Woodside dipped 0.6 per cent to $33.35, their lowest for six months, weighed down by a drop in crude oil prices.
Speaking to investors yesterday, Ms O'Neill declared oil and gas demand would remain "resilient" for decades, justifying backing new projects despite mounting pressure to decarbonise.
The 100,000 barrels per day Sangomar oil project in Senegal is due to start up in the middle of next year, at a cost of between $US4.9 billion and $US5.2 billion. That should be followed by the first cargo from Scarborough LNG in 2026 - barring further delays in securing regulatory approvals - and by the 100,000 barrels per day Trion oil project in Mexico in 2028, costing $US7.2 billion.
Ms O'Neill also reiterated her call for "a legislative fix" to remove the huge uncertainty hanging over the consultation required for offshore gas projects, warning ongoing delays will result in hits to jobs, tax revenues and energy security, and escalate the cost of living.
Scarborough and Santos' $US5.8 billion Barossa gas project in the Timor Sea have been mired in legal challenges and approval delays since a Federal Court ruling last year tossing out the regulatory endorsement for Barossa because of inadequate consultation with Indigenous communities.
Subsequent approvals have ended up in court, challenged by traditional owners through the Environmental Defenders Office (EDO).
Ms O'Neill, who is also chairwoman of the oil and gas industry association renamed Australian Energy Producers, expects ongoing legal challenges through the EDO.
"I think what we see from the EDO is they are going to challenge everything associated with Barossa and Scarborough, unfortunately."
She compared the government's broader receptiveness to new investment in oil and gas unfavourably to that of the Mexican government.

title: Climate activists berate AusSuper for Origin block
author: Angela Macdonald-Smith
full_text:
Origin Energy's biggest shareholder, AustralianSuper, has been described as "the worst climate blocker since Clive Palmer" after the fund resolved to reject a near-$20 billion takeover bid for the electricity and gas supplier.
The Nature Conservation Council of NSW has compared AustralianSuper's position on the takeover offer from Brookfield and EIG to Mr Palmer's successful efforts to abolish Australia's emissions trading system.
In a post on X, the group said that by blocking Brookfield's promised investment in clean energy of up to $30 billion, the fund was "playing the dirty side of the energy transition", and called on it to "get out of the way".
AustralianSuper, which says the offer remains "substantially below" its estimate of Origin's value, declined to comment.
Canada's Brookfield has pledged to invest between $20 billion and $30 billion in clean energy and storage through Origin's assets if the deal completes, a figure that dwarfs Origin's capex commitment in the area if it remains a standalone company.
In approving the transaction, the competition regulator determined that the takeover would accelerate Australia's energy transition and emissions reductions.
But AustralianSuper's rejection of the cash takeover bid for Origin makes it very difficult for the bidders to secure the 75 per cent shareholder approval they need at the November 23 vote to complete the deal.
Brookfield and EIG, a Washington DC-headquartered fund, last week raised their agreed offer for Origin by 8 per cent to $9.53 per share. But the new bid was swiftly rejected by AustralianSuper, despite recommendations to accept from the board, some analysts and proxy advisers.
Shares in Origin rose 1.2 per cent to $8.74 in a third day of gains.
Ord Minnett yesterday advised its retail investor clients to accept the sweetened offer, a change from its earlier recommendation to reject the original offer at the lower price.
Ord Minnett has about 7000 retail clients that are shareholders in Origin, believed to represent over 1 per cent of the register.
"The new price is 12 per cent above our standalone valuation for Origin of $8.50, which we consider a reasonable premium," Ord Minnett said in a letter to clients, noting that the revised price is also slightly above the top end of the independent expert's valuation of Origin.
"After recommending voting against the previous offer, we now recommend voting in favour of the Brookfield consortium's improved takeover offer."
Several shareholders have yet to decide how to vote.
"We haven't decided one way or the other what we are going to do yet," Jason Beddow at Argo Investments said. "We thought the price - once the independent expert's report came out - was fair. I wouldn't say it was a knock-out blow, so I think we need to consider it as a shareholder."
A spokesman for Betashares said its current view was to support the bid from Brookfield and EIG. "However, we'll consider the facts as they emerge and make a final decision closer to the date," he said.
The Nature Conservation Council said the board, independent expert Grant Samuel, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission and proxy adviser Institutional Shareholder Services had said the bid was "fair". "But @AustralianSuper is voting the shares of 1 in 10 working Australians to block the deal, without asking its members," it wrote in a post on X.

title: Why the fight for Origin is so heated:   Page Two
author: Jennifer Hewett
full_text:
The public brawling over Origin Energy's future ownership reveals how much is at stake in the shareholder vote on November 23.
Issues in play include arguments over the fate and rate of Australia's energy transition, the increasing power of industry funds, the declining number of major publicly listed companies, the global reach of private equity, the extension of the competition regulator's mandate into climate change policy and the significance of long-term ownership relative to short-term profit-taking.
Even so, the hostile reaction by Origin's would-be acquirers - Canada's Brookfield Asset Management and US based EIG Partners - to AustralianSuper's rejection of the bid is unusually overtly savage.
As prominent stockbroker and resolute opponent of the deal Angus Aitken points out, it's extremely odd to accuse Origin's biggest shareholder of "acting in a coercive manner" while also warning shareholders there's a high chance they won't see the $9.53 bid price again for some time.
Aitken argues that the real issue is all about fees - both for the bidders and for the investment bankers pushing the deal, in this case Barrenjoey and Jarden.
"This isn't about $9.50 v 50c higher deals," he wrote in yet another missive to clients yesterday.
"This is about big PE firms doing a lot of work over 12 months and seeing large potential long-term fees slipping into the ether."
With the board still backing the deal, it's certainly true AustralianSuper's firm opposition to the bid is the big obstacle standing in the way of it getting through.
The fund has since backed up its rejection by again buying more shares in Origin to take it from just under 14 per cent to just over 15 per cent - extremely significant in a scheme of arrangement requiring approval of 75 per cent of shareholders. Perpetual, which holds about 3 per cent, is also expected to vote against the bid.
The bidding partners are clearly feeling particularly aggrieved. They had hoped they had passed through the last major barrier when the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission gave its approval last month.
The ACCC ventured into new and disputed territory by citing an accelerated rollout of the energy transition under Brookfield's ownership as a reason for its approval on public benefit grounds. This was due to Brookfield's (non-binding) pledge to spend $20 billion to $30 billion on renewables and storage over the next decade.
Given the delays in the energy transition, particularly in the rollout of transmission lines, this level of investment may or may not prove realistic. The workings of the energy market repeatedly defy any manner of expert predictions. It's just as possible - in fact far more probable - that Origin Energy remaining in public hands will be easily capable of investing whatever capital that is required.
A publicly listed company would also be far more accountable and transparent about exactly what money it was actually investing.
It's certainly hard to see how the judgment on what will or won't happen fits easily within the regulator's competition mandate or any expertise in this area.
It's much easier to see why the bid partners will be keen to gain traction for emotive criticisms that AustralianSuper's rejection of the deal somehow signals the fund is blocking faster action on climate change concerns.
That's even though there is absolutely no indication of AusSuper having any such motivation or producing any such result in the domestic energy markets business wanted by Brookfield. And EIG Partners is obviously not planning on any decrease in LNG exports from Australia when Origin's stake in APLNG is the part of Origin it wants.
EIG clearly agrees with Woodside CEO Meg O'Neill. In an investor update yesterday, O'Neill said growth for demand for LNG in particular was expected to continue as buyers seek to secure supplies to support renewables as they decarbonise.
It's all part of the many countervailing forces, some unpredictable, that are currently influencing global energy markets. Energy Minister Chris Bowen gave yet another speech yesterday insisting Australia's target of having 82 per cent renewable energy by 2030 was hard but achievable although conceding the transition will be "messy".
That last description counts as polite understatement. It's also why the government would promote Brookfield's promise to spend tens of billions as evidence the transition is on track - in stark contrast to most industry players' views.
But despite all the noise, AustralianSuper is taking its own strong stand based on its considered view of the long-term value of Origin leading to its sizeable bet on the company's positive future prospects.
It also commissioned its own independent review, which backed up this analysis over the company's reliance on Grant Samuel.
In a statement released at the end of last month, the fund described Origin as having a "unique portfolio of market leading energy assets and an advantaged position to capture value from the energy transition".
These assets include Origin's 20 per cent stake in UK energy retailer Octopus, with its fast-expanding international customer base using its popular Kraken technology platform.
AusSuper also noted Origin's market-leading customer numbers and gas peaking generation as well as its renewables projects while saying Origin is well placed to take advantage of global LNG demand.
The bidders' interest in acquiring all of this led to its engagement with the company over a year ago, with the offer adding a decent premium to Origin's share price at the time. But over the course of this year, the view of energy markets and Origin's strong future growth makes all its assets under current management look extremely valuable to a sophisticated, credible institutional investor like AustralianSuper.
It's countdown time.

title: Silk Road odyssey:   KASHMIR TO LADAKH
author: Geoff Raby
full_text:
On his third visit to 'heaven on Earth', Geoff Raby returns to an ancient trade route.
British historian Peter Hopkirk's derring-do account of the "Great Game" first drew me in. The title of his history (published in the 1990s) echoed Rudyard Kipling's use of the phrase in his 1901 novel Kim, which had by then become shorthand for describing the 19th-century geopolitical rivalry between Britain and Russia in Central Asia.
His ragtag bag of explorers, local tribal traders, spies, spivs and ambitious officials, who played the Great Game in the Western Himalaya, did so in the most physically perilous conditions, seeking fame, glory and occasionally wealth. Battling acute altitude sickness and extreme cold on the world's highest mountain passes, they were guided and supported by traders whose families had navigated these commercial arteries for centuries.
Having travelled many birthdays with friends or lovers, for my 70th I was going solo, with space for reflection, reading and writing. I chose to enter my eighth decade on the Silk Road - my third ever trip here in as many years. The first was in 2020, just as COVID-19 was breaking out - a successful winter search to spot snow leopards.
The second, at the start of this year, was also undertaken in winter - to visit Pangong Lake, the scene of fighting between India and China in June 2020.
My ultimate destination this time was the Nubra Valley in northern Ladakh. Descendants of Xinjiang traders and their camels were said to be found there.
In the 1970s, Kashmir was a sort of mythical romantic destination for many intrepid travellers. It's always been a fraught region, and the Australian Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade's travel advisory still tells us not to go. Over the decades, this region has been subjected to constant periods of communal violence, sporadic terrorist attacks, and military conflict between India and Pakistan.
Starting my adventure in October with a few days in Srinagar (the largest city in Indian-administered Jammu and Kashmir) would help with acclimatisation for the five high-altitude passes that lay ahead. And it offered sufficient time to experience autumn in Kashmir - the ideal time to visit.
From September to November, dense vegetation on the steeply sloped hills is a variegated sweep of yellows, gold and browns. Late blooming flowers in old Mughal and colonial British gardens are a mass of colour. When I arrive, expansive Dal Lake is glistening.
My guide from January, Usman Qayoom of Kashmir Walks, is waiting at the airport to welcome me with an exaggeratedly colourful bunch of local roses. It's noon and the prayers from the muezzins have begun as we thread our way through the traffic.
It feels good to be back in a Muslim country. Since my first encounter with these incantations in Java nearly half a century ago, they always stir images of far-distant lands in hard-to-reach places; of unfamiliar customs and ritual.
It's a Friday, and Qayoom leaves to attend Friday prayers after he's dropped me off at the Karan Mahal Hotel, high above Srinagar on an old royal estate with uninterrupted views of Dal Lake.
The hotel is one of many gems to be found around Kashmir. Most visitors think of staying on houseboats, but other options are just as charming, and typically more comfortable. Built in the 1920s, Karan Mahal was the former residence of the Crown Prince of Jammu and Kashmir.
Modernised throughout, fit for a king, it is a veritable museum of 1920s and '30s interior design and decoration, surrounded by a garden and an old apple orchard.
Kashmir is captivating in so many ways, but it's the interplay of history, culture and religion that hooks you. Saffron - known locally as red gold - from Persia brought by Sufi saints turns fields purple in late October. Willow trees from England line water channels and streams, initially to provide valuable wood for building and for cricket bats, favoured by Sachin Tendulkar, the highest run scorer in history.
The pleasure gardens of the Mughal (Persian rulers of India) remain sanctuaries for calm reflection 400 years on, sporting ancient Persian chinar trees over 50 metres tall. Mosques based on square wooden designs adopted from Tibetan Buddhist architecture are unique to Kashmir and Baltistan in Pakistan, which were one before Partition in 1947.
Srinagar remains a popular retreat from the stifling heat and humidity across the north Indian plain that builds relentlessly until monsoon breaks, and Gulmarg (Meadow of Flowers) has become an attractive winter skiing resort.
But, it remains a city under occupation by security forces. Things have vastly improved, and Kashmir's tranquillity today contrasts with the "times of troubles", as locals call the period from 1991-2003. Secessionist movements, both home-grown and supported by Pakistan, conducted terrorist actions to which Delhi responded forcefully.
Security remains ubiquitous, but it has become like wallpaper against which people calmly go about their lives. As Qayoom says, his generation of those born in the early 1990s "grew up under the shadow of the gun". While residents still reflect on Kashmir's independent past, they want a more peaceful life. People are friendly and welcoming, and I felt safe.
A visit to Srinagar wouldn't be complete without at least one night on a houseboat. Like many romantic ideas, houseboats have their downsides, and not just in winter. Given you can only reach them by small wooden boats (shikaras) and an oarsman, they're inconvenient for daily touring.
I spend a night on the Mascot Houseboat. Comfortable and serving tasty home-cooked Indian meals on board, it's on Nigeen Lake, a bit out of town and quieter than the famous Dal Lake. Sunset brings families of chestnut teal ducks returning home, and in the morning shikaras drift by on the luminous surface, providing moments of ethereal transcendence.
Time passes quickly up here, and winter is coming. Leaving Nigeen Lake, we cross the Indus River, ascending the Sindh Valley - it's thick with conifers under the watchful eye of imperious 4760-metre-high Thajiwas Glacier. It's like Ticino, Switzerland, but on a vastly grander scale.
After lunch in Sonmarg, we ascend for over an hour, inflicting severe punishment on our vehicle's straining gear box as yet more vast mountainous vistas open up with every sharp switchback.
This is one of the world's greatest road trips. Closed half the year, the 434-kilometre road to Leh crosses three high passes that range from 3550 to 4078 metres - Zojila, Hambuting-La, and Fatula - and it's heavily used by trucks and military transports. Two days are a safe minimum; we take four, as there's much to see along the way.
Zojila Pass is known as "zero point" - the border between verdant lush Kashmir and the high-altitude desert of Ladakh; some 180 kilometres further east from the pass, Tibetan Buddhism takes over from Islam at Rangdum Monastery.
Next is Kargil - an important trade centre in the 18th and 19th centuries, it's now often left off tourist itineraries. The Silk Road Museum, reminders of the 1999 Kargil War, and the old town where now dilapidated caravansaries once accommodated weary traders are worth seeing. The Kargil Hotel (with its own bomb shelter) has a delightful garden, comfortable rooms and friendly staff.
Fourteen kilometres out of town, the Indian and Pakistani armies face each other along a 5000-metre-high ridge. The Line of Control marks the frontier.
Ibrahim, a resident from the bombed-out village of Hunderman, tells me he was 16 when war broke out. His village was shelled for four months and about 120 villagers sheltered in a cave perched above the valley floor. "Tribal people from the mountains share a bond with each other," says the guide employed by Qayoom for his specialist knowledge of the area. "Everyone has to pull together to survive."
Nearby is the Suru Valley, where, in the hamlet of Apati, you'll find a magnificent, 10-metre-tall and remarkably complete first-century AD sculpture of Maitreya, the Future Buddha.
To Kargil's north, after crossing Hambuting Pass, is the Aryan valley - infamous for Hitler's mad belief that the "master race" hailed from this beautiful, remote place. I saw no locals with blond hair or blue eyes, although a guide assured me they were there. Returning to Kargil, we stop to inspect another Maitreyan statue from the seventh century AD.
From Kargil to Leh, my new driver, Murtaza Ali, is a local Balti tribesman whose weathered skin and stoop belie his 42 years. Having driven these mountains for the past two decades, he happily navigates the most treacherous bends and knows every point of interest along the road.
Leh is home to about 31,000 people, of whom two-thirds are men. It's now effectively a garrison for the Indian Army to protect against Chinese border incursions.
On an east-west ridge overlooking the Indus River, to Leh's south, lies the huge Zanskar range. I spend a few nights at the Grand Dragon Hotel, each day waking to breathtaking views of its 6000-metre peaks.
Buddhist monasteries, temples and the ancient seat of government, copied from the Potala Palace in Lhasa, are east of the town. This area is littered with crumbling white stupas in their thousands. Leh is more Tibetan Buddhist than Lhasa today. Religious freedom in India allows for a more authentic Buddhist experience in Leh than in China-controlled Tibet.
With autumn well in retreat among the deciduous poplars and willows along the river, the background of high peaks makes for striking views. Climate change is being felt. Some 90 per cent of villages and farms in the region rely on water from glaciers that are shrinking rapidly each year.
In Leh, I reconnect with Noboo Tsering, who owns Snow Man Tours. A few years ago, he took me out to spot snow leopards. His knowledgeable guide, Gyatso, and Noboo's brother, Wang Chuk, this time take me deep into the Nubra Valley.
From Leh, a long day follows crossing Khardung La, the second-highest sealed road pass in the world at 5602 metres. It's snowing, making the trip more treacherous.
Nubra's expansive landscape is virtually beyond imagination. At its widest, it is two to three kilometres across a flat river plain, a U-shaped valley carved out during the last Ice Age containing the Shyok River rising in the Karakoram on China's border and the Nubra River fed by the Siachen Glacier on Pakistan's - the "world's highest battlefield". At a height of 6115 metres and 75 kilometres long, it is India's biggest glacier.
Stone Hedge Hotel at Hundar is a convenient base. An oasis fed by glaciers, surrounded by moraine, the hotel looks directly east towards a cluster of seven peaks over 6000 metres. The closest, Yamantaka, provides a spectacular canvas for the sun on which to paint its morning and evening colours. The hotel's deck is made for admiring Yamantaka, while nibbling momos (dumplings) from the outdoor kitchen.
Here our search for Bactrian camels begins. Truth be told, we don't have to look too hard - they're now a tourist attraction. Shafi, a fifth-generation descendant from Xinjiang merchants, explains that camels were not used in the high mountains between Leh and Yarkand. Wealthy Xinjiang merchants introduced them for personal transport. In 1959, when China closed the borders, families were stuck in Nubra. Some went to Leh or Kashmir, others to Turkey; many left their camels behind, ensuring a pool of breeding stock, the results of which delight tourists today.
Further up the valley is the start of the Silk Road route across the Karakoram mountains. Following the Nubra River north, after two hours is the hamlet of Sasoma, past which foreigners are forbidden. Here traders began their 30-day trek across the two major ranges to China. It was from this point that the first European explorers set off across the Western Himalaya in the 1850s.
It's now physically (and politically) unusable. Locals say along this route, bleached bones of the dead provide a trail to follow. High above the banks on a near-vertical wall, the old track remains visible - until it disappears behind a sharp ridge.
It's here we strike gold. Tsering Wangyan, a weathered 77-year-old Ladakhi, worked as a civilian for the Indian Army for 16 years, carting supplies along the fragment of the Silk Road we are now gazing at. He would make six trips a year to high-altitude military posts on the India-China border, his horse-and-mule train taking about five days.
Asked about Muslim descendants of former Silk Road traders, he tells a similar story to Shafi. Several Xinjiang families had settled in the region but fled to Kargil in 1949 fearing repatriation back to China. Chatting to Tsering through my guide Gyatso, the cold begins entering warm spaces, creeping across my skin with a tightening grip like a malicious vine. Here, in this desolate place, he seems like a tenuous link to a time when caravans of precious goods from Yarkand and Leh rattled across the high passes.
On the way back to Stone Hedge, we see urials, ibex and bharals (blue sheep), all favourite foods of the snow leopard.
On reaching the hotel, we're handed a message from Shafi that his 90-year-old father, Hadji Abdulah Razza Jamshi, is on his way to meet with us.
Sitting in the late afternoon sun on carpets from Khotan, eating dried fruit and nuts while sipping salted milk tea, Hadji recounts his life and family background. He was from the region - from a moderately wealthy family, he was educated, and worked as a teacher of Urdu until his retirement. With chiselled features, smooth skin and sparkling eyes, he's full of life.
Two years ago, Hadji published a small book on Silk Road traders now translated into English, in which he recorded the length and time each stage took from Sasoma to Yarkand. His own father had married a local Ladakhi and stayed, while many others accepted Turkey's offer of asylum. Some half-dozen descendant families remained in Hundar, but all are now mixed blood with Ladakhis.
Next morning, as we are preparing for our return to Leh, we hear that near Stone Hedge a snow leopard has just taken down an ibex, its carcass still warm.
The fringe of the Indian frontier is the edge of existence. What keeps me returning time and again isn't just the scenery, people, cultures, history, wildlife and physical challenges. It's the fact this region makes you feel small. It is, essentially, the exhilaration of insignificance.L&L
Geoff Raby travelled at his own expense. He was Australia's ambassador to China, 2007-11.

title: How green is my destination?:   THE HOT LIST ADVENTURE
author: Nina Karnikowski
full_text:
It's not easy going on holiday responsibly - but Nina Karnikowski has done her homework.
Travel accounts for at least 8 per cent of the world's carbon emissions, according to the World Travel & Tourism Council - a growing figure that is prompting many to zero in on how and why we venture overseas.
If sustainable travel matters to you, the best tip is to do your research. Think of the most environmentally responsible way you can travel, and support businesses that can prove they have a positive impact on communities and the environment.
In a world rife with greenwashing and virtue signalling, this isn't easy. Not least given the lack of government legislation and global eco standards that are easily identifiable and independently verified on an ongoing basis.
After you've waded through that minefield, consider whether "sustainable" travel is even enough in the midst of an urgent environmental crisis. Maybe you want to lean instead into "regenerative" experiences that go further towards funding the protection of nature and marginalised communities.
Here are 10 options backed by operators we like. They aren't perfect by any means, but they are making an effort to be transparent and accountable. Some are minimising their energy usage or using recycled materials, while others are focused on empowering local communities - and simply pushing guests out into the natural world, which is one of the best ways to help validate pro-environmental behaviours.
Community uplift | Botswana
21 Wilderness' Mokete Camp opens mid next year as a "placeholder" for the more permanent 10-room Meraka camp, due to open in 2026.
Mokete will comprise the only lodge in Botswana's 50,000-hectare Mababe Concession, a lesser-visited area of the African country situated on the eastern fringe of the Okavango Delta and the Moremi Game Reserve, to the south of Chobe National Park. In this concession, mega herds of buffalo, elephants and zebra roam, to name a few of the wildlife stars.
Wilderness began in 1983 when a group of like-minded African guides banded together. Today it operates in eight African nations, including Namibia, Rwanda and Zambia, and helps oversee about 2.3 million hectares of land. The company's "brand family" includes the non-profit community and conservation entities, plus a private airline.
Zimbabwean Keith Vincent is the chief executive, and the main shareholders are FS Investors and the Rise Fund - private investment entities that seek long and durable partnerships.
Wilderness vows to use tourism to help lift local communities by providing jobs, lease fees and small business grants.
Solar-powered Mokete Camp will have nine en-suite canvas tents (for a maximum of 18 guests) with retractable roofs for stargazing, plus a tented communal lounge and a pool.
■ Prices start at $US1145 ($1705). See wildernessdestinations.com or email enquiry@wildernessdestinations.com
Carbon offset | Iceland
22 Adventure holiday company Much Better Adventures helps clients travel with a clearer conscience by publishing the carbon footprint of each itinerary it offers. It also plants enough trees to pull at least twice the amount of carbon out of the atmosphere for every trip completed. It works with 100 per cent locally owned, independent businesses, so more of your travel dollars stay in the local economy. And 5 per cent of revenue goes to its conservation and reforestation-focused foundation.
Much Better Adventures has taken the added step of acquiring B Corp certification from not-for-profit global body B Corporation, which has been operating since 2006 to help companies and individuals hold themselves to greater account, while also supporting their efforts with a network of like-minded people.
Consider one of Much Better Adventures' new itineraries in 2024 - such as five nights of back-country hiking and wild camping in remote Iceland, trekking through canyons, past waterfalls and across lava fields in Vatnajökull National Park.
■ From $3446 per person, twin share.
See muchbetteradventures.com or
call +44 020 3966 7597.
Low-carbon ballooning | Stratosphere
23 Space tourism and the strongly associated chest-thumping billionaire space race will get a rebrand when the Céleste - a pressurised luxury capsule lifted by a gigantic balloon - launches into Earth's stratosphere, most likely late next year.
OK, it won't come cheap. But it's an interesting new product in the space tourism category.
Created by Zephalto, a low-carbon space travel company founded in 2016 by French aeronautical engineer Vincent Farret d'Astiès, the Céleste will produce just 27 kilograms of CO2 (equivalent to driving a car for about 110 kilometres) when it takes its six passengers to an altitude of 82,000 feet. While this is below the boundary of space, it will allow passengers to admire the curvature of the Earth, which astronauts have described as fostering a deep sense of interconnectedness.
■ The six-hour journey, including three hours of stratospheric floating, includes Michelin-starred dining and will cost $200,000 a person. Tickets and more information at zephalto.com
Sustainability focus | Manchester
24 Manchester is popular with
eco-minded urban explorers. This year, it was the site of the UK's second sustainable living festival, The Sustainability Show, and it's home to the 65-hectare Northern Roots, the UK's largest urban farm and eco-park. A few years ago, Manchester City Council released a blueprint to become net-zero by 2038 - 12 years ahead of the UK government's 2050 target.
Manchester will take another step towards that goal when the city welcomes the 216-room Treehouse Hotel at Deansgate in April.
This eclectic hotel, operated by luxury group SH Hotels & Resorts, is redeveloping the city's old Renaissance Hotel on the River Irwell - recycling the bones of an outdated brutalist building that many had considered beyond salvage.
The £200 million ($381 million) project will prove otherwise.
Treehouse Hotel will feature reclaimed and recycled materials throughout, including the furniture, and will operate using strict energy and carbon savings. Its sustainability practices are all listed on the website. Expect roof gardens, a rooftop apiary, indoor living green walls, a rainwater-fed kitchen garden and more.
■ From $380 per night, see treehousehotels.com/manchester
Wildlife education | Kenya & Tanzania
25 If you want to take more than a suitcase full of souvenirs home from your next holiday, luxury African safari company andBeyond's new WILDeconomy Masterclasses (just introduced) are food for thought.
The five-night, six-day experiences include discussions about the role of Africa's "wildlife economy", slotted in around the usual safari routine of game drives, walks and other activities.
On a WILDeconomy trip to Tanzania's Lake Victoria to be hosted by the Africa Foundation next year, for example, travellers will learn about the positive impact that sustainable fishing practices have had for both the lake and the local Lukungu community.
The masterclass will be hosted by Richard Vigne, executive director of the African Leadership University's School of Wildlife Conservation. It includes three nights at andBeyond Grumeti Serengeti River Lodge in Tanzania, and two nights at Kichwa Tembo Tented Camp in Kenya's Masai Mara.
■ Priced from $21,700 per person, twin share, departing October 30.
See andBeyond.com
Feed your soul | Central America
26 In 2022, Costa Rica generated 98 per cent of its electricity from renewables for the eighth consecutive year, a figure verified by the Climate Action Tracker, among other bodies. So it's a natural fit for global sustainable luxury hotel chain Our Habitas to open its first-ever property in Costa Rica early next year - with a focus on immersion in nature.
Habitas Santa Teresa will be located on the Nicoya Peninsula, on the Pacific Coast side of the country, and is fronted by a private surf beach, with dense jungle to the rear of the eco retreat.
It will feature 10 luxury canvas tents and 45 "low-impact" rooms - meaning they'll be built from regional, ethically sourced organic materials. Habitas will plant equal numbers of trees to offset the wood used in construction.
Guest adventures on offer will include underwater volcano snorkelling, horseback beach rides and waterfall hikes, as well as meditation classes and farm-to-table food.
■ From $632 a night, twin share.
See ourhabitas.com/santa-teresa, or call
+52 415 215 9399
Hang with the chimps | Uganda
27 Uganda has never pulled the same number of cashed-up Western tourists as the likes of Botswana, Kenya or South Africa. And yet, its location in the Great Africa Lakes region makes it one of the continent's most picturesque, wildlife-rich countries.
For a conservation-aware stay option in Uganda, put Kibale Lodge on your list. When it opens in May, Volcanoes Safaris' fifth property will help travellers enjoy the surrounds, while also educating them about the area's issues through visits to community and conservation projects. With lodges located in Rwanda and Uganda, Ugandan-owned Volcanoes Safaris is celebrating 25 years of operation this year.
Kibale Lodge will sit on 60 hectares, on a ridge-top site close to Kibale National Park, in the western part of Uganda, a five-hour drive from the capital of Kampala. The park is home to more than 1500 chimpanzees.
With just eight deluxe rooms and a single villa - all run off solar power and rainwater - Kibale Lodge will keep things small and responsible.
■ From $1897 a night, see volcanoes
safaris.com or email inquiries@volcanoes
safaris.com
Support artisans & craft | Colombia
28 Delightfully named Thread Caravan focuses on preserving heritage craft traditions and putting travel dollars directly into the pockets of locals. The company was started in 2014 by American Caitlin Garcia-Ahern, who is based in Mexico and has a background working in social development and not-for-profits in the United States. Overheads are kept to a minimum, given it's just Garcia-Ahern and one assistant running the show.
Thread Caravan puts together multi-day artisan workshops around the world, helping shine the spotlight on local craft communities. Think hammock-making workshops in Mexico, sailing and embroidery in Panama, or natural dyeing and back-strap weaving in Guatemala. (The latter involves weaving with a strap looped around your back, then tethered to a pole or tree.)
Thread Caravan's new six-day trip to the Colombian mountain town of Barichara departs in April, and includes indigo dyeing and paper-making workshops, visits to local ateliers, and hiking.
■ From $4430 per person twin share, see threadcaravan.com. Price includes boutique accommodation, most meals, all workshops and excursions, and carbon emission offsets.
Improved train journeys | Italy
29 International travellers are forecast to make 75 million trips to Italy in 2023, up from 56 million last year. To encourage travellers to explore the country with a smaller carbon footprint - and to give lesser-known regional destinations an economic boost - Italy's state-owned railway holding company Ferrovie dello Stato Italiane (FS Group) is launching a series of new and refurbished trains and itineraries, from now until well into next year.
In July, FS Group announced the creation of a new company, FS Treni Turistici Italiani (Italian tourist trains), to oversee the project.
Look out for the express and historical trains, which will consist of 1980s and 1990s wagons that have been upgraded in the Rimini railway workshops for tourist use. They will feature roomy luggage carriages for transporting bicycles, skis and vehicles.
Sustainable mobility, here Italy comes.
■ Visit fsitaliane.it
World's greenest countries | Scandinavia
30 With its generally progressive politics, high standard of living, and prioritisation of clean energy and environmental responsibility, Scandinavia has long provided a leading model of communal sustainability.
No surprises, then, that the top four spots in this year's Global Destination Sustainability Index, which ranks global destinations based on their sustainability performance, were Nordic. Sweden's Gothenburg came in at No. 1 for the seventh year in a row, followed by Oslo in Norway and Denmark's Copenhagen.
Finnish capital Helsinki took the most impressive leap, jumping eight places from number 12 to fourth spot - thanks to its commitment to inclusive (accessible) tourism, efforts to measure the carbon footprint that travellers leave, and its goal of becoming the world's most sustainable travel destination by 2025.
If you need yet another reason to visit the Finnish capital next year, there's also the fabulous food scene.
■ See visitfinland.comL&L

title: Water worlds:   THE HOT LIST CRUISE
author: Brian Johnston
full_text:
Brian Johnston reviews 10 new ships that are due to set sail next year.
Got your heart set on finally cruising the Kimberley next year? Book Seabourn Pursuit, or Paspaley Pearl by Ponant. How about a trip down the Douro? Australian-family company APT is putting its own built and operated river ship, the MS Estrela, on that fabled waterway. No matter where you yearn to voyage, these ships will allow you to travel in state-of-the-art style.
Such a pearler
31 Luxe French expedition company Ponant strengthened its longstanding ties to Australian pearl producers the Paspaley Group this year, offering guests on select Kimberley cruises the chance to fly into a pearl farm at Kuri Bay aboard Paspaley's vintage Grumman Mallard flying boats.
In late October, the pair announced joint operation of a 30-guest expedition motor yacht from June. The former Island Escape was snapped up for a bargain $5.5 million, a tenth of its value, in a bankruptcy sale.
Few details have been provided, but the reborn Paspaley Pearl by Ponant promises advanced environmental technologies, and lays claim to being the only boutique Kimberley motor yacht whose cabins are graced with private balconies.
■ Prices and itineraries are yet to be announced, but the ship will sail the Kimberley, Papua New Guinea and Raja Ampat, and the Spice Islands in Indonesia.
Roast pork and port on the Douro
32 APT launches its latest purpose-built river ship on Portugal's Douro River in June next year. MS Estrela will host 114 guests in suites that include balconies with slide-down windows that open up to the scenery.
A Sun Deck will have a swimming pool, putting green and al fresco bar, with seating and sunbeds for a grandstand view over the Douro River's plunging vineyards. Guests can dine on light meals in the lounge or on the deck, while the main restaurant will offer multi-course international menus with an emphasis on Portuguese cuisine.
■ Nine-day Douro Delights sail on September 5 and October 10, priced from $6195 per person. Beginning at Porto, it takes in the baroque town of Lamego, and vineyards around Régua and Pinhão. The journey finishes overland with visits to Spain's Salamanca and Madrid.
In pursuit of excellence
33 The 264-passenger Seabourn Pursuit launched in August; following short Mediterranean and Caribbean seasons, it will establish its expedition credentials by sailing the South American coast and on to Antarctica. It then explores Pacific Islands before arriving in Australia in June for a Kimberley season.
The all-suite polar-class ship is Seabourn's second expedition vessel. Those who crave adventure without sacrificing lifestyle will appreciate the attentive service, fine dining and interior design by Adam D. Tihany, notable for his modern romanticism and private-club feel.
Expect bespoke Italian furniture, Swarovski telescopes and even heated wardrobes, a blessing in polar regions. Seabourn Pursuit's superb art collection is exuberant and colourful, while the use of metal, wood and leather evokes the era of early polar explorers.
Expedition facilities include a Discovery Centre, kayaks, Zodiacs, and two six-person submarines. A 26-person expedition team of naturalists, historians and scientists accompanies voyages.
■ A 20-day Isles & Cultures of the Andesite Line expedition between Guam and Tahiti departing September 8 is priced from $23,579 per person in a Verandah Suite. It includes the opportunity for World War II wreck diving in Micronesia.
Wired for fun, especially at sunset
34 Celebrity Cruises' fourth
Edge-class ship (and by 20 metres its largest) is scheduled to sail from Fort Lauderdale on December 3 this year for an inaugural Caribbean season. The $US1.1 billion ($1.7 billion) ship carries 3260 passengers.
Don't expect the waterslides and razzmatazz of mega-ships. Celebrity Edge-class vessels focus on chic design and feel-good amenities such as an expansive three-storey spa, and the exclusive restricted-access resort-within-a-resort The Retreat.
Celebrity Ascent sees the return of sophisticated, light-flooded design features produced by a creative team that includes British designer Kelly Hoppen and American designer Nate Berkus. Big thumbs-up to the two-storey, Moroccan-inspired Sunset Bar at the ship's stern.
Ascent will have four main restaurants and eight specialty dining options. Especially notable is Le Voyage, the signature international (but essentially French-inspired) restaurant from Michelin-starred New York chef Daniel Boulud.
■ Try a classic Mediterranean itinerary, such as the 12-night Italy, France and Spain round trip ex-Barcelona. It departs September 2 and costs from $7620 per person in the superior Aqua Class, which has privileged access to the SEA Thermal Suite and exclusive dining at Blu restaurant. Highlights include Cadiz, Gibraltar and Rome.
Behold your new queen
35 Stop press. When magnificent Queen Anne sets sail on May 3, it will (appropriately) be under the command of female captain Inger Klein Thorhauge. It's also Cunard's first new ship in 13 years.
Queen Anne's international design team has a strong track record with high-end yachts and brands such as Nobu, Mandarin Oriental and Fortnum & Mason. Think classic glamorous Cunard style and art deco finishes combined with striking new design, bold colour tones and updated livery.
A prestigious, 134-square metre Queens Grill Grand Suite gets you access to your own reserved table at exclusive Queens Grill restaurant, where you can dine any time on dishes created by Michelin-starred chef Michel Roux.
■ A 13-night Singapore to Dubai cruise sails on March 25, 2025 with stops in Malaysia, Colombo and Abu Dhabi, and costs $13,699 in a butler-serviced Queens Grill Suite. Don't miss the fitness, beauty, thermal and spa facilities at Mareel Wellness & Beauty.
Ray of light
36 Silver Ray sails on June 3 from Southampton as Silversea's second Nova-class ship following Silver Nova's launch last August. Considerable effort has been put into sustainability. Advanced hybrid technologies and dual-fuel engines result in low emissions.
The 728-passenger ship has a novel asymmetrical design, such as a swimming pool set to one side of the pool deck. It retains Silversea's sense of elbow room and exceptional number of dining choices for its guest capacity.
Regulars will welcome the return of La Dame (fine French fare) and Kaiseki (Japanese). SALT Chef's Table is a new evening affair for 18 guests, offering a series of small plates that showcase local flavours.
■ Cruise Silver Ray's eight-day Cartagena to Lima journey departs December 27 next year and costs from $7550 per person. It transits the Panama Canal and visits Manta in Ecuador and Salaverry in Peru, with an overnight in Callao, Lima's port town.
Explore the world in style
37 The Aponte Vago family, owners of "mums and dads" MSC Cruises, has finally entered the luxury market with Explora Journeys, and two €500 million ($826 million) ships. Explora I sailed in August this year, with Explora II expected in August next year.
Both ships hold up to 922 passengers and notably abandon that staple of cruise-ship design, a main pool deck, instead offering three outdoor pools and a fourth indoors.
Six restaurants, a culinary school, casino and spa are among the amenities. The frisky will enjoy leaping from the spa's steam room to a salt cave to an ice fall, after which they can recover on heated marble loungers - or at the Malt Whiskey Bar.
If you only settle for the best, book an Ocean Residence. These apartments at sea range up to 149 square metres, with lounge and dining areas, bathrooms with heated marble floors, Frette linen, and an always welcome espresso machine. For anything else, ring the butler.
■ The 10-day Red Sea Kingdoms journey return from Jeddah in Saudi Arabia departs on November 12, and costs $18,300pp in an Ocean Residence. It visits Aqaba in Jordan (for Petra), Safaga in Egypt (for Luxor and Karnak) and AlUla in Saudi Arabia.
Oh-so Scandi chic
38 The number of Viking ocean ships hits double digits with the launch of Viking Vela mid-next year (the exact date has not been released). Viking's suave ships, which cost around €400 million ($660 million) each to build, have barely changed in terms of design since the line's first-ever ocean cruise ship, Viking Star, launched in 2015. But Vela will be slightly larger, carrying 998 passengers instead of 930.
All Viking's ships approach luxury levels in their all-inclusive fares, offering efficient service and considerable style. Expect no-fuss Nordic style without glitz. You'll appreciate the sense of space, the quiet ambience and nooks in which to unwind.
Vela (meaning a sail in Latin) will retain the venues that Viking regulars appreciate, such as the stylish indoor-outdoor Wintergarden with its striking beechwood canopy, and the spa with its skin-tingling Snow Grotto. The World Café offers an evening buffet, while Manfredi's specialty restaurant serves some of the best Italian food at sea. Vela's inaugural season takes it to the British Isles and northern Europe.
■ The 15-day Viking Homeland cruise between Stockholm and Bergen has several departures from May to August 2025, and takes in breezy Baltic cities and Norwegian fjords; from $9595 per person.
The grandest suites of them all
39 Sarah Fabergé, godmother of Regent Seven Seas Grandeur and a descendant of the renowned Russian court jeweller, Peter Carl Fabergé, will christen Regent Seven Seas Cruises' sixth ship in Miami next month.
The $US450 million ($700 million), 746-guest vessel takes Regent's signature opulence to the next level.
This includes lavish all-balcony suites, elegant public spaces and eye-catching artworks and - of course - a custom-made Fabergé egg.
Seven Seas Grandeur will also have an expansive spa, infinity-edge plunge pool, art deco-inspired observation lounge, and several fine-dining venues serving French, Italian and Pacific Rim food.
The 532-strong crew is one of the highest crew-to-passenger ratios at sea.
■ Who could resist an itinerary entitled Romance in Italy, Love in Spain? The 14-night return cruise from Barcelona departs on April 24, and costs from $21,120 per person. It will visit highlights such as Palma de Mallorca and Saint-Tropez, and overnights in Monaco.
Restyled and ready to go
40 Oceania Cruises spent $US100 million ($155 million) overhauling four previous ships, and this year was the turn of the Marina, which holds up to 1210 passengers. It will be relaunched this month.
The mid-size liner was built in 2011. Its staterooms and suites have been entirely refitted, and luxury levels upped with the use of Italian marble, bespoke fabrics and custom-crafted furniture.
The soft furnishings of the ship's public areas have also been renewed, with some restaurants and bar spaces restyled.
Oceania is known for its casual elegance and attentive service. Many consider it to offer the best overall dining experience at sea, extending to the classy buffet in its casual Terrace Café.
■ Head to far-northern Europe on a 15-day Glaciers and Greenland cruise between Tromsø in Norway and Reykjavík in Iceland, which departs
August 5 and costs from $10,020 per person.
It takes in the remote Norwegian polar-bear destination Svalbard, four locations in Greenland, and Iceland's Grundarfjordur. L&L

title: SLOW CHANGE IN FAST FASHION
author: Lauren Sams
full_text:
Sustainability Eva Kruse says legislators must force clothing brands to go green, writes Lauren Sams.
Things are simply not moving fast enough.
"I have been championing this agenda for almost two decades and I am still surprised at how slow it is," she says. "Conversation stays at the 'nice to have' level. We like to do the little things we can do, within our parameters, to stay comfortable."
It is a straightforward but damning statement on the state of an industry that is known to be a significant polluter.
Fashion uses large amounts of water, land, chemicals and energy, as well as human labour. It relies heavily on plastic (more than half of all clothing is made from synthetic fibres, usually polyester-based) and, with profit driving businesses, it has been resistant to change.
Kruse, a self-described "stubborn optimist" believes it can be done.
"There is a mechanism in fashion that we have created for ourselves, where we are constantly chasing the new," she says. "During COVID-19 there was a movement to rewire the industry, to produce less, to have fewer fashion weeks, to have a longer shelf life for products.
"That disappeared when borders opened. But the questions remain. Why do we drop spring products in winter and then discount the winter products? It's bad for business! We need products for a reason, not a season."
Kruse has been at this for a long time. A former magazine editor and television host, she founded Copenhagen Fashion Week in 2005, which has become the world leader in sustainable fashion.
Kruse then founded the Copenhagen Fashion Summit (now known as the Global Fashion Summit) and Global Fashion Agenda in 2009, and worked with the United Nations on the Sustainable Development Goals for businesses.
Kruse left the Global Fashion Agenda in 2021 and is now chief global engagement officer at Pangaia, a material sciences company that uses its innovative fabrics in loungewear and activewear, selling them to fund research into more sustainable practices (especially raw materials).
She believes that sustainable fashion is not a philosophy but a business model, one that will be as valuable to shareholders as to the planet.
And to do that, Kruse says we need legislation and tax to change the system.
"We can do a lot as an industry, but ultimately we need legislation to step in," she says. "There is, at maximum, 50 per cent of the fashion industry that is moving in this space. And most of those players are doing business as usual, and making only very small amounts of change."
I mention Seamless, an initiative of the Australian Fashion Council that proposes a four cent levy on all garments imported here. She mulls it over.
"There is no magic wand we can swing to solve the climate crisis, but without a doubt, heavily taxing carbon will do the most. If you hit people on their wallets, you will make impact."
Though she believes that it's important for consumers to "hurt a little bit", Kruse is hesitant to place the burden on individual shoulders.
"The consumer shouldn't be taxed, it's the provider, the producer [who should be]," she says.
Convenience and price are important, she adds, with "sustainability way down the list of priorities" for most people.
"So it belongs to the industry to make a better product. And those that are unwilling need to be pressured by legislation."
Kruse herself is a fashion lover. She is wearing Alexander McQueen heels (bought on Vestiaire Collective, a resale site) and activewear from Pangaia. She understands that fashion is, for many of us, spirited and frivolous.
"We shouldn't take away that fashion is fun, creative, an industry full of ingenuity," she says. "It should be exciting. It's a cultural indicator, it tells the story of who we are. It's not the newness in itself that's wrong, it's how much newness there is."
The frustratingly slow pace of change is at odds with the ever-faster growth of most fashion companies, she says.
"The elephant in the room is the constant pursuit of growth, which is fundamentally ingrained in our society," she says. "Success means growth."
She understands the economic reality at play.
"For publicly traded companies, there are shareholders, I get that," she says. "For any business, there is the need to pay your staff. But we need to have a discussion about what creates value, and it doesn't necessarily have to mean volume."
Kruse wants to create a more circular industry, where "every product has value".
It's through this approach, she says, that we can build a profitable system that doesn't continually require new materials, more energy and resources like water and land.
"We need to remember that every product has value," says Kruse. "Maybe it's lost value for you but maybe for someone else it has value, or maybe the raw material has value." Circularity can become a profitable business model, she says.
"The largest environmental footprint issue is materials, and circularity can help with that. It requires systemic change and sentiment change. We need take-back systems, we need to incentivise business and consumers to return things and also to consume things that are not new, but new to them. But it's very promising."
Ever the stubborn optimist, Kruse often comes back to an early life lesson instilled by her father.
"It can be overwhelming," she says. "You can think, 'Who am I, what can I do that matters?' I remember as a teenager, not wanting to go to a march against nuclear power with my dad. I said, 'What does it matter if I don't go?' And he said, 'What if everyone said that?' So I went.
"It matters what you spend your money on, almost more than who you vote for. How you live, what you do on a daily basis, these things are very important. It's the cumulative power of everyone's actions, individuals and businesses, that will really make change."W

title: Virgin steps up Boeing MAX buys:   Aviation
author: Ayesha de Kretser
full_text:
Virgin Australia has ramped up its investment in new, more fuel-efficient planes as Boeing puts the biggest of its next generation MAX aircraft into flight testing.
The IPO hopeful said on Friday it had ordered six more Boeing 737-8 MAX aircraft, bringing its total to 39. It received the third of 14 737-MAX 8 planes from Seattle on Friday, with the remainder due to arrive in 2024.
The 737-8 MAX planes will fly on Virgin's domestic network and short-haul international routes including Fiji, Bali and Samoa. "These new aircraft enable both significant growth and improved fuel efficiency," Virgin said in a statement. "New MAX 8 aircraft will reduce emissions by at least 15 per cent per flight compared to older generation 737s," supporting the airline's carbon reduction target.
Virgin is aiming for a 22 per cent reduction in emissions by 2030 and aims to achieve net zero emissions by 2050. The new planes are also 40 per cent quieter.
Virgin has also ordered 25 of Boeing's newest 737-10 MAX planes, with delivery expected to begin in 2025. On Thursday, the US Federal Aviation Administration gave approval for the manufacturer to start flight testing, which was delayed after two fatal crashes related to the 737 MAX invited heightened regulatory scrutiny.
A spokesman for Boeing said the airline welcomes the FAA's decision clearing it to begin certification flight testing. "With more than 400 flights and nearly 1000 flight hours, the 737-10 continues to perform well as we prove out its safety, reliability and performance through a rigorous testing and certification process," he said.
The MAX 10 is the biggest in the next generation and will reduce emissions per seat by 17 per cent, Virgin said.
The airline will also start work on a $110 million fleet refurbishment program to install in-seat power for all passengers, as well as updated business-class cabins and more overhead locker space. The investment in new fleet and refurbishments comes as Virgin's private equity owners Bain Capital try to convince local fund managers to participate in its forthcoming initial public offering, slated for May.

title: ALL AT SEA ON SONAR INCIDENT
author: Andrew Tillett
full_text:
Naval skirmish The government looked flat-footed after an "interaction" between Australian and Chinese warships injured an Australian sailor, writes Andrew Tillett.
On the same day a Chinese warship's sonar pulses injured an Australian navy diver, Anthony Albanese was posing for pictures with Bluey and Bingo at the ABC's annual showcase at Parliament House.
The Prime Minister was skewered when he posted a picture to his X (formerly Twitter) account, slammed for hobnobbing with kids TV characters while Australians were doing it tough or Gazans were being buried under rubble.
Albanese and the rest of the government kept quiet about HMAS Toowoomba's "interaction" with the Chinese destroyer Ningbo, lest it overshadow Australia's rapprochement with Beijing, with the Prime Minister meeting Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the APEC leaders' summit.
The incident was finally revealed last Saturday morning in a press release by Defence Minister Richard Marles, after Albanese wrapped up his pre-departure press conference from San Francisco. Journalists accompanying the PM received the press release as they were waiting on the tarmac to take off.
Albanese eventually addressed the incident on Monday, condemning it as dangerous and reckless. He dodged questions on whether he had raised it personally with Xi. Complaints were made through diplomatic channels.
"This incident occurred within the Japanese exclusive economic zone; it's not exactly a piece of contested waterway somewhere nearer to the Chinese coast."
Jennifer Parker, a former naval officer who is now a director of defence policy at ANU's National Security College, says universally recognised flags and signals would have been displayed showing diving operations were under way as divers cleared fishing nets off the propeller.
She says one thing that is not clear is whether the Chinese warship turned its sonar on as it approached the divers, or already had it on as it sailed around looking for submarines.
"There is a conversation around is it intentional or is it incompetency?" she says.
Nevertheless, the government's handling of the incident has been bewildering. While confrontations between Australian (and Western) militaries with Chinese forces in the South China Sea and East China Sea are commonplace, this was the first time Australian personnel had been injured (the diver has since recovered).
It was hard not to think back to Scott Morrison's angry reaction when a Chinese bureaucrat circulated a doctored image of an Australian soldier slitting an Afghan child's throat. Morrison arguably handed the Chinese a "PR win" by taking the bait but he left no doubt that he backed the troops.
"I can tell you from long experience that Defence Force personnel will be very attuned to that," former Defence Department deputy secretary Peter Jennings says of the government's response.
"They will be seeing it as the government sends us into harm's way but the government won't back us when we're under attack," he says. "There is a real threshold test there about supporting the Defence Force and the PM's failure to do it is a bit of a Rubicon and will be seen that way by Defence."
Jennings, now head of Strategic Analysis Australia, says it was a political misjudgement by Albanese and the government not to protest more forcefully about the Chinese warship's actions. "If there was ever a time to push back against China and use the Albanese phrase of 'disagree when we must', this was that moment," he says. "It was a badly handled example of how 'stabilisation' is really about Australia kowtowing to China in return for trade."
But former Australian ambassador to the US and Japan, John McCarthy, says Australian protests over the interaction were best made at senior defence officials level, especially because of the technical maritime aspects involved, rather than a leader-to-leader exchange.
"It's not good but has to be kept in proportion to all the other balls in the air," McCarthy says. "A lot of things are not dealt with at leader-to-leader level. It seems to me this is the sort of issue that I would have thought was best dealt with navy-to-navy, followed up with the defence secretary or defence minister if necessary."
While the view from within government was it would have been counterproductive for Albanese to directly challenge Xi over the incident, the PM noted in an interview it had been a setback. "The consequences of these events are that they do damage to the relationship. And this certainly is an event that does do damage. And we've made that very clear to China," Albanese said.
The confusion over the government's response points to the fundamental tension in Australia's China policy, which, as Marles articulated this week, is a source of both wealth and anxiety.
Albanese, Foreign Minister Penny Wong and Trade Minister Don Farrell deserve credit for stabilising the relationship, helped by Beijing's realisation that beating up on everyone was a dead end.
The various trade sanctions have largely melted away, while ministerial and diplomatic dialogue and visits have resumed.
But the government continues to send out mixed signals on defence and security policy.
Albanese pulled off a coup with the treaty with Tuvalu, which gives Canberra an effective veto over the tiny nation's security relationships in return for a climate change lifeboat, amid China's unrelenting efforts to gain a security foothold in the Pacific.
And he took Labor all in on AUKUS and its $365 billion price tag for nuclear-powered submarines.
But nine months after the AUKUS announcement, key decisions such as who is going to build them are yet to be made. Sources say the government is also unhappy with the recommendations of the surface fleet review - which outlines the new warships the navy needs - and is now trying to wrangle it into something more palatable.
Marles - who has privately indicated he needs an extra $25 billion to pay for new weapons - is said to be frustrated he hasn't been able to convince colleagues to boost defence spending even further despite the frequent warnings of how dire the strategic outlook is.
"Defence is just not priority," Jennings says. "There are obviously significant numbers in Cabinet that don't accept the argument China is a strategic threat to Australia or at least one that requires a military response."
Meanwhile, despite Canberra's relative restraint over the sonar incident, China went on the front foot. Chinese state media and officials suggested HMAS Toowoomba had been sailing in contested waters, while insisting the Ningbo had kept a safe distance and did not conduct any activities that affected diving operations.
"We urge the Australian side to respect the facts, stop rude and irresponsible accusations toward China, engage in endeavours that are conducive in boosting mutual trust, and build a positive atmosphere for developing better bilateral relations and military-to-military ties," Chinese National Defence spokesman Wu Qian said.
Australia is not alone in rousing China's ire over matters maritime. The Pentagon estimates there have been almost 300 clashes, confrontations and interactions between western warships and aircraft with Chinese forces in the Indo-Pacific since mid-2021, part of Beijing's "grey zone" campaign which stops short of military action.
Overlapping claims between China and its neighbours for islands, rocks and shoals, and the territorial waters that surround those features abound in the South China Sea and East China Sea. While Taiwan is the biggest flashpoint, probably the greatest risk of a physical clash at the moment is between the Chinese and Filipino navies.
A fed-up Philippines president Ferdinand "Bongbong" Marcos Jr this week basically called time on lengthy negotiations for a maritime code of conduct between South East Asia and China. Instead, he will turn his attention to bilateral codes with fellow ASEAN members.
"As I have said before, and I will say again, the Philippines will not give up a single square inch of our territory to any foreign power," Marcos told a forum in Hawaii on Sunday.
Japan - which this year established a military hotline with China to minimise the risk of clashes in the disputed Senkaku Islands, which Beijing claims as the Diaoyu Islands - and the US both slammed China's actions towards HMAS Toowoomba.
Lowy Institute China expert Richard McGregor says the incident shows that no matter how good Australia-China relations will be, "it's not going to change Chinese behaviour in areas where they are determined to assert their influence".
"The kind of behaviour we see from the People's Liberation Army Navy I doubt is directed from on high in a technical sense but Xi Jinping and Chinese leaders have decided they will try to drive foreign navies away from China's shores as they can, even if that means harassing them in international waters."
The Australian navy, for its part, hasn't been bowed. An Australian warship - HMAS Toowoomba - sailed down the Taiwan Strait on Thursday.P

title: Green efforts offset by our coal
full_text:
Driving through Central Queensland recently, I was struck by the size and frequency of the massive coal trains that ran alongside the Bruce Highway. This coal was being sent by rail to Dalrymple Bay and then by ship to our export markets. During 2020-21, Australia produced 11,894 petajoules of coal, with 10,324 PJ of that exported. Only 14 per cent of our coal production is consumed domestically. Aside from the COVID-affected year of 2020-21, the increase in coal exports over two decades has dwarfed the reduction in coal consumption due to shuttering Australian coal plants. However, the government consistently sidesteps including coal exports as part of environmental discussions.
For all the investment and effort Australia has put into reducing greenhouse gas emissions, 10 times the amount of environmental damage has been caused by our additional coal exports.
Instead of following the Australian lead, our customers are eager to burn all the coal we can send them.
Adrian Tilley
Carindale, Qld
Pledge funds at COP28
As the government wrestles with fossil fuel phase-out, there is concrete action that Chris Bowen can take to build Australia's climate credentials at the COP28 talks in Dubai.
Climate change has already wreaked devastation across the world, causing irreversible loss and damage, and dealing a huge economic blow, particularly in low-income countries. Loss and damage funding needs for low-income countries are estimated at $US400 billion a year.
Funding needs will only grow if ambitious action is not taken in line with the Paris Agreement target.
Australia has played an important leadership role as a member of the loss and damage transitional committee. The government must provide an urgently needed financial contribution, in line with like-minded countries including the US, the European Union, Britain and Canada.
Australia could step up and make an initial pledge of $100 million to the Loss and Damage Fund at COP28.
Pacific communities are looking to Australia for global leadership on loss and damage, and this would be a concrete sign we are serious, alongside any regional initiatives we support.
Marc Purcell
CEO, Australian Council for International Development
