title: Australia's alternative energy brawl spills over at meeting:   Technology
author: Hans van Leeuwen
full_text:
Dubai | Australia's domestic debate over nuclear energy has spilled over into the COP28 climate summit in Dubai, as the opposition set out its stall and drew flak both from the government and Liberal Party dissenters.
Opposition climate change and energy spokesman Ted O'Brien is leading a delegation of Liberal and National parliamentarians to COP28 for a five-day visit focused heavily on promoting nuclear energy as a future part of Australia's energy mix.
He vowed that in government the Coalition would join a 22-country partnership pledging to triple nuclear energy capacity by 2050, which was inked during COP28. And he expanded his party's nuclear vision to include potential grid-scale reactors in NSW's Hunter region and other former coalmining areas.
But Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen launched a blistering broadside against his opponents, describing the nuclear policy as "a pipe dream". And senior Liberal figures at COP28, including former prime minister Malcolm Turnbull and former NSW treasurer Matt Kean, questioned the policy. Simon Holmes a Court, the bankroller of teal electoral campaigns, also queried whether nuclear was right for Australia, although he backed a big expansion of nuclear energy worldwide as part of the fight against climate change.
"COP28 will be known as the nuclear COP," he said. He described the Coalition's policy as an "all of the above" plan, involving renewables, coal, gas and nuclear.
Speaking to reporters after his speech, he said the Coalition would not support the COP28 pledge, signed by more than 100 countries, to triple the world's renewable energy capacity.
"What we don't need is all of our eggs in one basket. We need a balanced mix of technologies, and that includes renewables," he said. "But we also have to keep open-minded, that includes other technologies. The days of pitting technologies against each other as a fight have got to be over."
On nuclear, Mr O'Brien envisioned a role not just for small modular reactors that can be used for mines, city-level power or industrial processes, but for big reactors to firm up renewable electricity's intermittent, variable feed into the grid.
"When it comes to nuclear technologies, we are looking at all-of-the-above for generation three-plus and beyond. So that is micro reactors, that is small reactors, that is large reactors," he said.
Mr Bowen responded that at COP28, "nuclear energy is not involved in the multilateral conversations. When I meet with counterparts, even those who are nuclear countries, they say 'if I had your renewables, your renewable potential, I wouldn't go down the nuclear road. It's a pipe dream wrapped in a fantasy accompanied by an illusion ... and I don't have time for distractions."
Mr Bowen and Mr O'Brien have been facing off over nuclear policy for months, but each has found what might seem like potentially unlikely allies at COP28.
Former Labor cabinet minister Joel Fitzgibbon backed the Coalition's proposal to scrap the ban on civil nuclear energy in Australia.
"Just lift the prohibition and let the market decide. If it can't get community support or attract capital, so be it. But let's find out" he told The Australian Financial Review.
Mr O'Brien pointed to international studies showing that countries using nuclear were typically decarbonising more quickly, and said the government was going down a path that would not deliver net-zero.
"It's a fact that nuclear is one of the fastest ways to decarbonise a grid," he said. "Of the top 10 case studies for decarbonising grids at speed, half of those come from nuclear energy.
"You want to do it fast, you do it with nuclear."
Mr Holmes à Court, convener of Climate 200, backed the push to get more nuclear energy onstream globally. "We hear from many this week that with electrification, the world is going to triple its electricity demand by 2050. So tripling nuclear by 2050 is running to stand still."
But he said it was "hard to see where nuclear fits in in Australia" for the immediate energy transition, because 80 per cent of Australian coal would be out of the grid by 2035 and nuclear would not be onstream before 2040.

title: The three who have the fate of the ANZ and Suncorp deal in their hands:   DUE DILIGENCE
author: James Eyers
full_text:
The 20 lawyers representing ANZ, Suncorp, the competition regulator and Bendigo and Adelaide Bank had to battle a big media pack last week as they entered the Federal Court in Sydney's Queen's Square.
But the cameras and microphones were not looking for the silks and law firm partners attending a special hearing of the Australian Competition Tribunal. The media throng was there for the defamation action brought by Bruce Lehrmann against Network Ten and Lisa Wilkinson, which was taking place on the 22nd floor.
So the banks' legal teams were able to move into to the ceremonial courtroom, on the floor below, unnoticed. But they, too, were entering a cauldron, a legal battle where the stakes are also sky-high. It was unclear who was winning at the end of last week, in a dispute that will define the competitive boundaries of the banking system for years to come.
On February 20, the fate of ANZ's $4.9 billion takeover offer for Suncorp Bank - blocked by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission in June - will be decided by this tribunal, comprising a Federal Court judge, an economist and a company director.
If the tribunal decides the same way as the ACCC - that the deal will substantially lessen competition in the home and agricultural lending markets - there will be egg on the faces of ANZ boss Shayne Elliott, and his counterpart at Suncorp, Steve Johnston.
A defeat will send ANZ back to the drawing board to recover lost market share in Queensland, and leave Suncorp saddled with a subscale bank, which will be on the table for another acquirer, potentially Bendigo Bank.
But if the tribunal gives a green light to the deal, this will create a lasting legacy for Elliott and Johnston.
It would allow ANZ to create a new platform for growth in Queensland and overtake National Australia Bank as fourth-biggest housing lender. It would free up Suncorp to focus on its insurance business and the rising risks of climate change. Overturning the competition regulator would also trigger big fees for investment bankers withheld if the deal fails.
With the strategies of both companies on the brink, the atmosphere in the courtroom was serious and reserved.
The case has ended up in this room because the ACCC did not buy ANZ's arguments that Suncorp's banking division would only provide an incremental lift in market share, so would not reduce competitive intensity for home loans and rural lending. Instead, the ACCC's merger team blocked the deal for further entrenching the banking oligopoly and the likelihood of encouraging more co-ordinated behaviour between the major banks.
The hearing kicked off last Monday with Ruth Higgins, SC, presenting ANZ's case. She has been briefed by an Ashurst team led by partner Peter Armitage. The in-house work is being led by Roslyn Moloney.
Higgins declared competition alive and well. "There is no reason to believe this will collapse into consumer or competition inertia" if the deal was allowed, she said. The ACCC decision had been divorced from the reality, she argued, given the ongoing influence of mortgage brokers, while the regulator had displayed "diffident non-satisfaction" (legal speak for a lack of confidence) when it rejected the takeover.
The tribunal is rehearing the case, using the same arguments made to the ACCC. That means it is not looking for some error made by the regulator, like an appeal court would when seeking to overturn a lower court; rather, it is bringing fresh eyes and minds to re-decide the case, using the same law.
On Tuesday afternoon, Cameron Moore, SC, took the lectern to outline Suncorp's case. He had been briefed by Linda Evans, now at Herbert Smith Freehills (which she joined in 2021, after a long career with Clayton Utz). Belinda Speirs, a former Suncorp general counsel now group executive of completion and transition, is taking the lead internally, and was exchanging post-it notes with Evans last week.
A lot of last week's evidence involved commercially sensitive information, resulting in the hearing entering closed sessions for most of Thursday and Friday. There's also confidential information including board papers from other banks, their views of competition in the mortgage markets, the impact of the deal on prudential safety, that has been taken privately.
The lawyers' picnic will continue through to Friday this week. Bendigo Bank will continue arguing its case today. It is using law firm Webb Henderson, led by partner Andrew Christopher, who has briefed Nicholas De Young, KC. Mr De Young explained on Friday afternoon that Bendigo and Suncorp bank would be a good strategic fit.
The ACCC is expected to follow Bendigo, from tomorrow to Thursday (ANZ and Suncorp will reappear on Friday if all goes to plan). The ACCC has been briefed by the Australian Government Solicitors, with a team of five barristers led by Garry Rich, SC, and Robert Yezerski, SC.
Queensland is represented at the tribunal by a team from Corrs Chambers Westgarth, led by partner Michael Kimmins.
Once the silks knock off on Friday, the future of the deal will shift to the three members of the panel the tribunal formed to adjudicate. The group is being led by John Halley, SC, a relatively new judge, hearing his first tribunal case. Justice Halley was appointed to the Federal Court in March 2021 after 13 years as a silk specialising in competition and commercial law, including many cases involving market power and merger clearances.
The other panel members are Jill Walker, an economist and long-time tribunal member who has been a commissioner at both the ACCC and the New Zealand Commerce Commission, and Diana Eilert, an experienced director and executive, who is on the board of Domain and is chairwoman of Keypath. Interestingly, Eilert used to run Suncorp's insurance business, and has also managed its people and technology functions. (The parties were asked whether they had any objections to her participation and none did.)
The three will be preparing a decision by February 20. The only appeal avenue for the parties will be through administrative law, should the tribunal make some error of law. Absent this, neither ANZ, Suncorp nor the ACCC will be able to object.

title: CEOs say red tape threatens new investment
author: James Thomson and Anthony Macdonald
full_text:
Some of Australia's top energy and resources leaders including BHP's Mike Henry, Lynas Rare Earths' Amanda Lacaze and Santos' Kevin Gallagher say the threat to investment from higher interest rates is compounded by rising costs, activism and unfriendly government policies that could push capital offshore.
"In addition to capital costs going up, policy changes at both the federal and state level are exacerbating the problem by creating further cost increases and greater investment risk. These will be a negative for business investment in Australia," Mr Henry told The Australian Financial Review's annual Chanticleer CEO Poll.
"Many other nations around the globe are pursuing policies that make them more competitive and more investment friendly. Capital will flow to where the best risk and returns exist and the opportunities elsewhere are looking increasingly more compelling," he added.
Ms Lacaze said Lynas would further invest for growth but investing in Australia was not getting easier. "It is important that all governments remember that capital is mobile and decisions to invest in Australia will only be made where we have a consistent policy framework under which to operate," she said.
"Australia presents itself as a low-risk jurisdiction, particularly for the minerals industry. However, some recent policy decisions at both federal and state level challenge this assessment particularly where policy changes have been made with little or no effective consultation.
"Investment decisions will always be made rationally and capital will not be deployed where there is uncertainty about significant policy changes."
Santos CEO Kevin Gallagher said higher rates would lead the LNG giant to "prioritise the lowest risk and highest return investment opportunities" but also said the country "is still in the midst of an anti-fossil fuels war when the real enemy is emissions".
"The rising impact of activism in Australia is one factor in addition to inflation that we need to consider going forward," he added. "Investments will be prioritised for lower risk regulatory environments. There's a real competition for capital across our portfolio, and we will continue to invest where it makes economic sense and the returns are highest."
Australia's official interest rate has jumped 4 percentage points since May 2022 to 4.35 per cent, ending almost seven years of rates below 2 per cent.
"When the cost of debt is higher than the return of equity, the investment balance is wrong and makes it incredibly difficult to commit significant amounts of capital."
Steve Donohue, chief executive of Endeavour Group, said higher rates had led the liquor retailing and hotels giant to reconsider some investments.
"We've made a conscious decision in the short term to take stock, look at our existing portfolio of hotels, and prioritise their improvement ahead of material acquisitions in the short term," he said.
"In effect we've shifted the focus to get more out of what we've already got which may result in a slightly lower overall outlay for a better return."
Viva Energy's Scott Wyatt was one of several chief executives to note rising rates are not the only thing stopping investment.
"It is driven by more than just cost of capital - expansion of project delivery costs, and a greater uncertainty on project timeframes, are major factors impacting deliverability and does impact forward-year planning," he said.
Wesfarmers chief executive Rob Scott said higher rates could actually throw up some opportunities for the giant conglomerate.
"Investors that rely on financial engineering and high leverage to do deals are less competitive, so we are starting to see more value emerge," he said, adding that the cost and availability of capital was just one factor impacting investment at the group.
Environmental processes, regulatory issues, the availability of skilled labour, international competitiveness and taxation are also factors he was watching, Mr Scott told the survey.
"For example, a delay in project approvals by a year or two, combined with additional costs navigating complex regulation or dealing with labour shortages, can turn a good investment opportunity to a value destroying one, and all these factors are independent of interest rates."
While infrastructure projects have been hit with the double blow of rising interest rates and higher construction costs, Chris Ashton, chief executive of engineering giant Worley, said the urgency of the energy transition means demand remains robust.
"Like any business an increase in inflation and interest rates has an impact on costs," Mr Ashton said.

title: Voters think ALP is failing on most fronts:   Report card
author: Phillip Coorey | Political editor
full_text:
Cranky voters believe every key area of government focus has got worse over the past year, except for the relationship with China.
The latest The Australian Financial Review/Freshwater Strategy poll shows voters believe that everything from wages to the economy, energy bills and the behaviour of politicians has deteriorated.
Of the 10 key parameters tested, the only cause for optimism was the bilateral relationship with China.
Of this, 54 per cent felt it was improving, while 45 per cent felt it was worsening or unchanged.
This gave it a net positive of 9 per cent, growing from 2 per cent when last tested in December 2022.
Stabilising the relationship with China was a signature achievement of the Albanese government in 2023, marked by Beijing lifting almost all the $22 billion in trade bans it had imposed, and by Anthony Albanese becoming the first prime minister in six years to visit China.
Other than that, people are down on the government.
Two-thirds, or 67 per cent, believe household finances are worsening, up from 56 per cent a year ago.
Despite the government making wages growth a central plank of its efforts, public opinion has worsened from minus 6 per cent to minus 18 per cent.
The government also joined forces with the states in the May budget to provide discounts for power bills. The poll found 70 per cent felt affordability was worsening, which is on par with the 69 per cent a year ago.
The biggest shift was a net 25 point increase in those who felt the behaviour of politicians had worsened, jumping from minus 14 per cent a year ago to minus 39 per cent now.
There was also a large net 20 per cent jump in the number of voters who felt the transparency of political decisions had worsened. Mr Albanese came to office vowing to restore standards of behaviour and discourse.
Climate change optimism has also dipped sharply, with views on Australia reaching net zero emissions in 2050 dropping from a net 20 per cent last year to 5 per cent now.
The online poll of 1109 voters was taken from Friday to Sunday and has a margin of error of 3 per cent.
It showed Labor had lost its lead and was now level with the Coalition on a two-party preferred basis at 50 per cent apiece. If an election were held today, the government would most likely be pushed into minority.
Mr Albanese's personal ratings had also plummeted over the past 12 months.
Asked yesterday "How will you regain your mojo?", Mr Albanese did not dispute the premise of the question. He all but confirmed there would be more cost-of-living relief next year, similar to or the same as the power bill discounts which Treasury said helped lower inflation.
"We'll continue to examine ways of taking the pressure off Australians whilst not also adding to inflation," the prime minister said.
He attributed the decline in his personal ratings to the ravages of inflation. "During an inflation issue that has affected the entire globe, there was obviously going to be pressure on the economy," Mr Albanese said.
"But what we've done is to create 700,000 new jobs since we came to office, we've continued to prioritise providing that support, $23 billion in cost-of-living support, while we found $50 billion in savings, turning around a $78 billion deficit into a $22 billion surplus.
"It is getting the big calls right that matter for this country, and that is what we are doing."

title: Dutton's political tactics are not a governing agenda:   The AFR View
full_text:
Just past the halfway mark of the Albanese government's first term, the political popularity contest is even-stevens, with Labor and the Coalition tied at a 50-50 two-party preferred vote, according to The Australian Financial Review/Freshwater Strategy poll published yesterday. Labor's slender 51-49 lead in the previous poll in September has evaporated after losing two points off a primary vote that has slipped to 31 per cent, lower than the 32.6 per cent received in the federal election in May last year. The Coalition's primary vote rose two points to 39 per cent, which is well above the 35.7 per cent of first preferences cast for Scott Morrison. That Labor has lost its lead for the first time since winning power is a measure of the government's bad end to 2023 amid the messy handling of the High Court's indefinite detention ruling. It is also a measure of Peter Dutton's political opportunism, such as the populist attack on Labor over the post-pandemic migration catch-up, which the poll suggests has helped push up to 60 per cent the proportion of voters who believe immigration levels are too high.
Mr Dutton will take heart from Anthony Albanese's approval rating slide and a marked improvement in his personal standing with voters. Mr Albanese's shrinking lead as preferred prime minister is also evidence Mr Dutton is not as "unelectable" as some pundits claim. But let's get real here. Nineteen months after being turfed out of office, the Coalition has made up ground as Labor is marked down amid the cost-of-living crisis - which remains by far voters' No. 1 concern - and the aftermath of the failure of the Voice referendum. Yet, the polls still suggest that the best the Coalition can hope for, which would be the worst outcome for the country, is Labor being forced into minority government at the next election.
With no real plan for winning back the six formerly safe Liberal inner-city heartland seats won by teal independents last year, there appears to be no realistic prospect at this point of achieving Mr Dutton's declared aim of a one-term return to government. More importantly, the Coalition's political tactics, such as petty weaponising of the prime minister's necessarily busy overseas travel schedule, offer no genuine governing strategy to deal with the big challenges such as net zero, productivity and budget repair.
The Coalition has seized on voters' power bill shock to push the small nuclear reactor option to generate affordable, reliable and zero-emissions electricity. Yet it has also revived the climate wars by opposing Labor's expansion of the Abbott government's de facto carbon price safeguard mechanism to help drive the lowest-cost, most efficient decarbonisation of the economy.
Australia needs to reverse its post-pandemic productivity slump to help the Reserve Bank finish the job of bringing inflation down. But apart from opposing Labor's retro union-ordered workplace re-regulation, the Coalition has no real industrial relations policy to speak of to help lift productivity. On the budget, the Coalition accuses Labor's "overspending" of adding to inflation. But it has not backed restoring the medium-term fiscal framework of balanced budgets over the economic cycle that the Morrison government ditched during the pandemic.
The problem for the country with the Coalition's tactics of opposing much and proposing little is that the political heat is not being put on Labor to genuinely revamp its policy approach in the new year. Off the back of mid-year economic and fiscal outlook showing the budget is most likely on track for a second small surplus in a row, Jim Chalmers used last week's interview with The Australian Financial Review to talk up the prospect of Australia following the US back to low inflation and lower interest rates next year. What this upbeat assessment underscored was Dr Chalmers' concern that responsible economic management will be the election-swinging issue.
With our poll showing Labor has now ceded its rating as the better economic manager as the cost of living bites, the treasurer is out there rebranding various government initiatives as Labor's plan to "modernise our economy". But this is just a poll-driven political exercise to try to paper over Labor's lack of a fair dinkum economic reform agenda, which is a bipartisan problem shared with Mr Dutton and the Coalition.

title: No excuse for male Chook pen
full_text:
Isabella Bruckback makes a valid criticism of the lack of women among the nine past and present Chanticleer columnists at the column's 50th anniversary lunch on Thursday last week ("Room for all in the Chook pen", June 18).
In my welcoming remarks to the "Chook" lunch, I said there was no excuse for this and it needed to change.
In the meantime, I added, it was balanced by all three of our Street Talk team being women, led by long-time column editor Sarah Thompson; by our two other daily columnists being Jennifer Hewett and Karen Maley; and by a majority of The Australian Financial Review's senior editors' group being women, including editor Fiona Buffini and managing editor Cosima Marriner .
In my weekly note to subscribers on Friday, I added that recent Chanticleer columnists had been champions for getting more women into Australia's boardrooms.
And I urged subscribers to watch out for next week's announcement of the winners of our new Women in Leadership awards.
My thank-you note to staff about the success of the lunch said that I and other senior editors encouraged everyone in the Financial Review newsroom to set high aspirations for their careers, including for big jobs such as Chanticleer.
Michael Stutchbury,
Editor in Chief,
The Australian Financial Review
There's no need for
renewables subsidiesA recent article pointed out the inconsistencies in the cost comparison of nuclear and renewable energy in the CSIRO's latest GenCost report ("The flaws in CSIRO's anti-nuclear, pro-renewables report", June 13).
There is also a major inconsistency between the GenCost results regarding the requirement for renewable energy subsidies and the continuing government announcements of large-subsidy programs to promote investment in renewables.
The major conclusions of the GenCost report are that the costs of integrating variable renewables are "without any government subsidies" and that renewables, with integration costs, are the lowest-cost options of all new-build generation technologies.
Thus, according to the CSIRO, integrated renewables are the lowest-cost option without the need for subsidies.
If the CSIRO is correct, there is no need for subsidies to achieve the 2030 target of 82 per cent of power generation from renewables. Thus, the federal and state governments can safely dismantle the subsidy regime and rely on market forces.
Although it does not adversely affect the achievement of the target, eliminating the unnecessary subsidies would greatly reduce the cost burden on electricity consumers and taxpayers.
David Carland
Milsons Point, NSW
Polls show Labor
is fooling no oneLabor's hypocrisy on inflation is probably poisoning its credibility and polling ("Middle-income women deserting Albanese", June 18).
State and federal Labor shed crocodile tears on wanting to fight inflation while refusing to index land tax, super and tax bracket thresholds.
Their deliberate intent is to profit handsomely from the inflation that they themselves continue to fan with their inflationary fiscal policies, leaving mortgage holders to carry the pain of higher interest rates.
As Abraham Lincoln said, you can't fool all of the people all of the time.
William S Lloyd
Denistone, NSW
Surgeons' high pay
is a doctored effortI was not surprised that surgeons are the highest-paid occupation by a considerable margin.
Their incomes are mainly funded by the taxpayers and health fund premiums.
It is undeniable that to be a surgeon takes many years of training and requires great skill ("Australia's highest-paid jobs revealed", June 18). Surgeons must receive adequate compensation.
However, it is also true that the Royal Australasian College of Surgeons has control over the supply of surgeons.
Restricting their supply, or that of any other occupation, increases the income of those who benefit from this monopoly.
The rest of society bears the cost.
I am sure that there are many general practitioners who would have the ability to be surgeons, especially female doctors who are woefully under-represented.
Barry Lizmore
Ocean Grove, Queensland
No national movement is beyond criticismThe article by Amie Frydenberg is fascinating ("Zionism is about Jewishness. Anti-Zionism is antisemitism", June 18).
According to this Zionist logic, being anti-Islamic State or anti-Saudi regime is also discrimination against all the 1.9 billion Muslims, since Islamic State as well as the Saudis have invoked the religion and indeed have a verse from the Koran on their flags.
One may argue the case that "Zionism is about Jewishness" but it doesn't mean Zionism replaces Judaism. Indeed, there are more Christian Zionists than Jewish ones.
Regardless, Zionism started as a national movement to establish a Jewish home.
Making an exception for one ideology is hypocritical, to say the least.
Any national liberation movement, right or wrong, has a right to exist. But no national movement has a right to become holy and beyond criticism.
Palestinians have their own national liberation movement, which has been in existence since before Israel was established.
Are we also to consider that movement as holy and beyond criticism?
Assad Abdi
Sydney, NSW
Dutton needs energy policies that stack upPeter Dutton's leadership of the opposition must surely be up for questioning ("Dutton's climate war spells trouble for Labor", June 13).
He advocates for the highest-cost energy system as his big power solution while claiming, without support, that renewables will somehow go from being the cheapest form of energy to suddenly "explode" in price and "grow exponentially".
To further claim that Monique Ryan is "completely disconnected" is, for a Kooyong resident, quite beyond belief.
Ryan is probably one of the most connected MPs - with strong, mutual engagement with the electorate she actually represents, as opposed to just blindly supporting party policy.
If he wants to offer himself as an alternative prime minister, Dutton should provide policies that stack up under scrutiny and make statements that are credible.
His nuclear nonsense utterances are not going to cut through in this country.
If he wants to differentiate himself from government energy policy, he could investigate and promote an acceleration of the renewables and storage roll-out, including Long Duration Energy Storage as a concept.
Robert Brown
Camberwell, Vic

title: Fallman heads trio of locals promoted by Brookfield:   Street Talk
author: Sarah Thompson, Kanika Sood and Emma Rapaport
full_text:
Canadian private capital giant Brookfield has dealt promotions to three of its most senior employees in Australia as part of a broader push to beef up its presence in the region, Street Talk can reveal.
Sophie Fallman has been named head of Brookfield's global client group for APAC. The new title is expected to put her front and centre of the firm's efforts to raise funds across the region, sources said. She'll also be tasked with deepening relationships with Brookfield's private institutional investors, which have ploughed more than $US60 billion ($89.5 billion) into its strategies.
Brookfield has been pivoting its Australian real estate portfolio towards alternative sectors since 2018, sinking more than $14 billion into senior living, student accommodation, logistics, office and mixed-use assets.
Fallman had been head of the real estate group since 2018 and with the firm since 2010. Her appointment comes after US-based David Levi was named chief executive of Brookfield's global client group earlier this year and instituted a regional model for client engagement, opening the way for a vacant APAC position.
In response, head of real estate investment for Australia, Ruban Kaneshamoorthy, has been appointed head of Brookfield's property group, responsible for investment and asset management. He and Danny Poljak, the current head of Brookfield Properties Australia who has been with the firm since 2004, will now work as co-heads of the firm's Australian real estate business and seek to grow its footprint.
Kaneshamoorthy was head of investments for Brookfield's real estate group in Australia, reporting to Fallman. He and Poljak will report to Brookfield's real estate head of Asia Pacific and Middle East, Ankur Gupta.
Late last month, the Canadian property giant put much-loved Sydney landmark Luna Park on the market. The firm is also seeking to buy France's Neoen, which could see it emerge as the largest owner and operator of renewable energy in Australia.

title: Grok woos US families for Sun Cable
author: Primrose Riordan
full_text:
The head of Mike Cannon-Brookes' private Grok Ventures says wealthy American families are "really interested" in backing the $40 billion Sun Cable project, which will supply Northern Territory solar power to Singapore.
Tan Kueh, a former Macquarie and BlackRock investor, said she had been in the United States drumming up support for the project and for a broader pivot to open up the billionaire Atlassian co-founder's family office to outside investors.
Ms Kueh, in her first interview since being appointed five months ago to oversee Grok's shift in strategy towards only green investments, said the difficulties of financing clean energy projects reminded her of her work on another asset class - infrastructure.
"I was at Macquarie fairly early in the days of infrastructure becoming an asset class ... it's sort of not dissimilar to that time," she said.
"How do you have to go about raising capital for something that doesn't necessarily have an operating history, that banks don't know how to lend to, [that] people don't know how to assess and value and risk."
Grok has about 10 full-time staff, including chief investment officer Jeremy Kwong-Law and Goldman Sachs' former head of venture investments, Lucinda Hankin.
The Australian Financial Review's Street Talk column revealed last year Grok would stop investing in listed equities to focus on decarbonisation.
The change of strategy meant the departure of Grok's global equities portfolio manager, Armina Rosenberg, who had been hired to diversify Mr Cannon-Brookes' wealth away from Atlassian, the New York-listed technology platform he founded with Scott Farquhar in 2002.
Grok has previously held stakes in Alibaba, Apple, Amazon and Netflix.
"Mike is a really important investor, [but] other investors will also be seen to be important as well when they come in the future," Ms Kueh said, describing the firm as Grok 2.0. It would only invest, however, when returns were high enough.
"A lot of climate capital is still associated with blended capital ... meaning not 100 per cent necessarily commercial outcome seeking capital," she said.
"Think of us as people who want to ... exploit climate investing as a commercial and investible opportunity."
Grok has about 24 investments in its portfolio. Ms Kueh said it had made more than $1 billion in investments, without revealing details of its funds under management or rate of return. Aside from Sun Cable, the most notable is its 10.4 per cent stake in AGL Energy, along with toilet paper retailer Who Gives A Crap, solar farm developer Quinbrook, infrastructure debt provider Infradebt, and renewable energy fund Solar Bay.
Mr Cannon-Brookes has previously described AGL - where he thwarted a plan to split generation and retail into two companies - as "one of the most toxic companies on the planet".
But Grok has become more conciliatory in its approach over the past year.
Shareholders, including Mr Cannon-Brookes, spared the company a second strike and abstained from a vote over its remuneration last year while saying the "carbon transition metrics" in the report were not ambitious enough.
Ms Kueh said she would take a "collaborative" approach and said "no" when asked if she agreed with Mr Cannon-Brookes' assessment.
"You will struggle to get one of those descriptors out of me," she said. "We have to work together ... otherwise we're not going to solve this climate problem."
At Sun Cable, Ms Kueh said there was a need for "lots of money, huge amounts of money".
The ambitious venture involves building a 20-gigawatt solar farm near Tennant Creek in the NT, an 800-kilometre overhead transmission line to Darwin, and a high-voltage undersea cable for the 4300-kilometre link to Singapore.
Grok acquired it after the project fell into administration after a disagreement between Mr Cannon-Brookes and his joint venture partner, Fortescue executive chairman Andrew Forrest. It has previously been budgeted at $40 billion.
"We met with a lot of investors and big families," Ms Kueh said of her recent trip to New York, San Francisco, Chicago and Silicon Valley. "People were really interested in it."
The project team is working through regulatory approvals and "ticked boxes" to allow outside investment. Ms Kueh visited Singapore to meet energy officials earlier this year.
"The next milestone we get to [is] where there is enough de-risking that has happened ... that we can actually get other people interested in participating on the journey with us," she said. She said there had been "accelerated progress" over the past few months.
"The bulk of the green energy that's generated from the site is actually going to be used domestically. I think a quarter of it is going to be potentially shipped, exported," she said.
"But the rest of it is going to be used to power local industry and green manufacturing."
Mr Forrest had lost confidence in the export part of the project, preferring to focus on solar generation in the NT and use that power to produce green hydrogen, while Mr Cannon-Brookes had been a supporter of the original vision for the venture.

title: LNP to debate nuclear despite agenda omission:   Exclusive
author: James Hall
full_text:
A senior federal Queensland MP has warned that the party faithful will be "white-hot angry" if the Liberal-National Party's state convention omits debating nuclear energy this weekend.
The alternative energy source has been left off the official running sheet for the three-day event in Brisbane, which the LNP hopes will serve as a celebratory launch for state leader David Crisafulli ahead of the October state election.
But the omission of nuclear from the more than 170 resolutions has perplexed Queensland's federal Coalition MPs, given the energy pitch has become a headline election policy for Opposition Leader Peter Dutton.
They insist the energy source will be keenly discussed and debated despite efforts to minimise conflict between the federal and state branches following Mr Crisafulli's refusal to support the policy.
"I'd be very surprised if there wasn't a single branch, SEC [State Electorate Council], FDC [Federal Divisional Council] or others that hadn't put forward a nuclear resolution," Mr Pitt told The Australian Financial Review. "There's been one at every convention for as long as I can remember, so that would be a shock."
Another MP told the Financial Review the omission "begs the question" whether a nuclear resolution had been put forward and rejected during the selection process by the agenda committee. "It does seem a bit unusual that there wouldn't be any," they said. "It's intriguing for me because cost of living and energy are virtually one and the same at the moment, but energy is a very big issue for us federally.
"I know a lot of people are passionate about it [nuclear], so it not being on the agenda is intriguing."
Mr Crisafulli's repeated refusal to support the nuclear push has infuriated federal party figures, including Nationals leader David Littleproud and most vocally MP Colin Boyce, who previously said the state leader should "put his big girl pants on and face the energy issues".
But state party figures are eager to hose down any suggestion of conflict.
They told the Financial Review the event would serve as a crucial opportunity for members to see "there's no bad blood" between Mr Dutton and Mr Crisafulli at the LNP's last convention before both the Queensland and federal elections.
Canberra-based insiders also said there was an acceptance among the federal branch to provide Mr Crisafulli with the latitude he needs to emerge victorious in October and form an LNP government in Queensland for the first time in nearly a decade.
"The rank-and-file membership are nuclear supporters [but] David Crisafulli just doesn't want that as a state election issue," the insider said. "We're mature enough to get that and not hate him for it."
The state opposition leader has placed the LNP in a potentially victorious position - according to a range of polls - by ruthlessly prosecuting the Labor government on crime, housing, cost of living and health.
State Liberal-National MPs fear a prominence on nuclear energy serves as a distraction from those Queensland-based issues. They insisted to the Financial Review they were "totally" united behind Mr Crisafulli's anti-nuclear stance.

title: Brookfield to sell Vic Neoen assets to seal ACCC tick:   Renewables
author: Angela Macdonald-Smith
full_text:
Canada's Brookfield has started early talks on the sale of 2.8 gigawatts of proposed wind farms and battery projects in Victoria in an effort to pre-empt competition objections to its $10.6 billion takeover of French renewable energy developer Neoen.
The offer of projects - including the proposed Moorabool battery near Geelong and the Navarre and Kentbruck green power hubs - is understood to have attracted keen interest from prospective buyers. A formal sale process is expected to get under way early next month before final bids are due in about November.
The proposed divestment was revealed in broad terms by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission on Friday when it kicked off an inquiry into the takeover deal, asking interested parties whether the combination of Brookfield's and Neoen's businesses across different parts of the electricity supply chain in Australia would damage competition.
Brookfield sealed the takeover accord in late May, agreeing to buy out the major shareholders of Paris-based Neoen, one of Australia's biggest developers of clean energy assets that will help replace ageing coal plants.
That acquisition of a majority stake will be followed by an offer for the remaining shares at the same price, with the aim of securing 100 per cent ownership.
The ACCC inquiry is the most advanced of several competition regulators across the globe that are set to examine the deal, given Neoen's operations that stretch across Europe, North and South America, in addition to Australia and Zambia. In Australia, Neoen has more than four gigawatts of clean energy and storage projects either operating or in construction, and is aiming to reach 10GW by 2030. Brookfield would retain Neoen's portfolio of 653 megawatts of installed wind, solar and storage capacity in Victoria,
Of particular interest to the watchdog is the potential impact from having common ownership of both generation plants and electricity transmission in Victoria, given the infrastructure giant already owns grid operator AusNet. It also zeroed in on Brookfield's control of Spain's X-Elio, which has one operating solar farm in Queensland and several development projects along the eastern seaboard, and asked whether X-Elio and Neoen compete in the supply of electricity to the market.
Historically, the ACCC has required generation to be held separately from network assets, to prevent a situation where a grid owner could give unfair advantage to its own generation assets in terms of accessing the network, to the detriment of other plant owners and therefore to competition.
"We are seeking your views on whether the proposed acquisition would be likely to increase Brookfield's degree of vertical integration in the electricity sector in such a way that substantially lessens competition," the ACCC said in its letter.
The watchdog noted that Brookfield has offered to resolve any competition concerns by selling Neoen's development projects in Victoria, and by measures that would separate the management of Neoen and AusNet in Australia.
Brookfield offered a similar undertaking on management in its earlier $20 billion bid for Origin Energy, which was approved by the ACCC last year but eventually rejected by Origin shareholders, led by the largest investor, AustralianSuper.
The Canadian company declined to comment on Friday on the competition inquiry, but Neoen chief executive Xavier Barbaro said last month in an interview that the deal parties were willing to be flexible to get the transaction over the line.
"It's important ... that we come up with ideas or solutions, and that we hear what the ACCC wants us to do," Mr Barbaro said, while adding that the regulatory approval was primarily a question for Brookfield.
"We will do what it takes to obtain those green lights. We are willing to be flexible and to find solutions for whatever challenge we may see."
Any agreement for the sale of the Victorian portfolio would be conditional on ACCC approval of the takeover. The ACCC asked for responses from interested parties to its inquiry by July 26, ahead of a decision provisionally set for October 3.

title: Albanese assault on Qld battleground:   Fortress state
author: James Hall
full_text:
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese launched a three-day pre-election assault on Brisbane this week, confirming the city's inner and suburban electorates as a key battleground in the looming national poll.
Queensland has typically been dominated by the Liberal National Party, where the Coalition occupies 70 per cent of the seats. But Labor is desperate to pierce the conservative fortress to protect the government's slim majority amid fears the LNP will increase its electoral footprint in other states.
Abolishing the Labor-held seat of Higgins in Victoria, as proposed by the Australian Electoral Commission, further threatens the government's majority.
Mr Albanese's pseudo-campaign-launch tour was in Dickson on Friday, the north Brisbane electorate held by Opposition Leader Peter Dutton, to spruik Labor's chances of flipping the tightly held seat.
The prime minister confirmed that Ali France would once again contest the electorate after trimming Mr Dutton's margin to just 1.7 per cent in 2022.
On Thursday, Rowan Holzberger was confirmed as the candidate for the commuter corridor seat of Forde in Brisbane's traditionally working-class south. In 2022, he halved the margin held by the LNP's Bert Van Manen to 4.2 per cent. On Saturday, Mr Albanese is set to unveil Labor's candidate for the seat of Brisbane, where the party came within just 11 votes of securing the second position in 2022 and winning on preferences.
Despite Ms France's ambitious bid to unseat Mr Dutton being more difficult given her rival's ascension to the position of party leader, Mr Albanese insists the electorate is in play.
"We're giving them a choice here in Dickson of voting for Ali France and saying enough is enough," he said. "At the last election, Ali achieved a swing of almost 3 per cent in this seat.
"This seat now has a margin of under 2 per cent - a swing of half of what she got last time will see Ali France elected."
The prime minister's Queensland offensive ahead of the national election, due by May, comes less than a week after nearly 1000 LNP members flocked to Brisbane for its state convention.
At the conference, Nationals leader David Littleproud and Mr Dutton spruiked the Coalition's nuclear energy plan and the latter stepped up his attacks on the prime minister, who he said had "no positive message" to convey after two years in government.
LNP strategists stress Queensland's significance and recognise the Sunshine State as the key battleground to force Labor into minority government.
"Queensland LNP really is the only reason why the federal Coalition is even half-competitive at the moment," a party insider in Canberra told The Australian Financial Review recently.
"Retaining that strength is absolutely critical."
The prime minister will return to Queensland next week to announce more federal candidates, Queensland senator Murray Watt confirmed.
"By the end of next week, he [Mr Albanese] will have announced more candidates in Queensland than any other state for the next election," he said.
"That's a deliberate choice to demonstrate that we're serious about performing here."
Senator Watt said there was "no doubt" Brisbane and regional Queensland would be an important battleground.
"The sheer number of LNP members across Queensland is a real challenge ... but the reality is quite a number of those seats are held on very small margins."

title: Stock picker tipped in $24m Darling Pt sale
author: Bonnie Campbell
full_text:
Luxury listings Geoff Wilson has joined the trophy home rush.
As the well-heeled jet off for their winter break, the usually rapacious trophy home market in Sydney's eastern suburbs has gone into hibernation ahead of the spring selling season.
However, there are still signs of life at the pointy end.
Take private equity deal-maker Potentia Capital's Andy Gray and his wife Emma, who recently sold their Darling Point luxury apartment in Sydney's eastern suburbs for an undisclosed sum, tipped to be more than $24 million.
Billed as "echoing the grandeur of a Manhattan penthouse", the parallels to New York end with the distinctively Sydney views of the Harbour Bridge and Opera House.
The chic interiors across two levels totalling 340 square metres of living space are the work of Dylan Farrell Designs.
High-end finishes include European oak parquetry flooring, marble bathrooms and a tailored dressing room. Other features include al fresco terraces, a chef's kitchen with Gaggenau appliances, a wine cellar and a Tesla charging point.
The buyer is tipped to be none other than stock picker turned trophy property collector Geoff Wilson and his wife Karen Greer, who appeared in AFR Weekend just last week after spending $46 million collecting Noosa holiday homes in Sunshine Beach.
No word yet if the rumoured purchase means the founder of ASX-listed Wilson Asset Management will be putting his nearby Double Bay home - bought for $10 million in 2010 - on the prestige market any time soon.
The two-storey, harbour view apartment hit the prestige market around seven months ago with $25 million to $30 million hopes. The property has been listed with Highland Double Bay's Bill Malouf, who could not be reached for comment.
The Grays bought the four-bedroom trophy apartment from luxury car dealer Robert Damelian and his wife Karen for $12 million in 2021.
The Damelians created the oversized offering by amalgamating two separate apartments - the first from cattle exporter Patrick Purcell and the second from Lynette Harvey, former wife of retail billionaire Gerry Harvey.
In the boutique block, the Wilson-Greers will join upstairs penthouse owner, writer Melanie Hershon, the daughter of the late rag trader Michael Hershon, of Hestia-Berlei lingerie fame. Ms Hershon paid $5.3 million for the penthouse to former owners, arts philanthropists Simon and Catriona Mordant, in 2012.
Other freshly minted Darling Point locals include Michael and Svetlana Huljich, of New Zealand's ultra-wealthy Huljich family.
The couple recently settled on a three-storey Yarranabbe Road duplex for $14 million.
The property was sold by Julia Cooney, daughter of renewable energy boss Jim Cooney, also through agent Highland's Bill Malouf.
Back in 2022, Emma and Andy Gray sold their grand Victorian Italianate mansion Rothesay in Bellevue Hill for $37 million to Adani chief financial officer "Robbie" Jugeshinder Singh and his partner, hedge fund sales consultant Marijana Domazet.
However, the Grays' hefty capital gains appear constrained to the eastern suburbs, given they recently sold another trophy home on Sydney's lower north shore for a $1.75 million loss.
That property, the Mosman Federation home known as Cambria, was purchased for $17 million in July 2022 and sold for $15.25 million in November last year.
Masterchef 'curry king'
steps up Mosman digsCashing in on the Grays' loss is new owner and former Masterchef contestant Jimmy Seervai, who has emerged as the Cambria's buyer following its May settlement.
Seervai is no stranger to the blue-chip suburb, having paid $11.6 million for a nearby home on the Balmoral slopes in 2020 - a decade after he hit Australian screens on the reality cooking show where he was dubbed the "curry king" for his spicy dishes, and placed fourth after winner Adam Liaw.
However, Seervai also appears to have copped his own Mosman property loss, given he sold his Esther Road home in February for $10.43 million - more than $1 million below his 2020 purchase during the pandemic property boom.
A trained food scientist, Seervai capitalised on his Masterchef profile to grow the food manufacturing business Essence Group, which sells sports supplements and nutritional products such as gummies to corporate giants including Woolworths and Aldi, as well as exporting them to the US, China and India.
Franklins' life-changing
Gold Coast hinterland
Retired AFL great Buddy Franklin and his model and businesswoman wife Jesinta have listed their Gold Coast hinterland home, known as Villa Casa, about two years after they bought the contemporary resort-style mansion for $8.75 million.
Speaking exclusively to AFR Weekend, Jesinta said the decision did not signal a return to city life, after leaving Sydney's east ahead of their interstate relocation in 2023 to the hinterland suburb of Reedy Creek, about a 15-minute drive from Burleigh Beach.
"Definitely not Sydney, that chapter is well and truly closed for us," Jesinta said of the prospect of returning to the Swans' territory where Lance retired soon after injuring his calf in Sydney's round-20 win over Essendon last year.
Now, the high-profile pair are looking to expand their footprint and give their children a taste of country life.
"Both Bud and I grew up rurally, so it feels right to return to what we know and give the children the same childhood we had," she said.
Lance grew up in Dowerin, in the central wheat-belt region of Western Australia, while Jesinta grew up in the Gold Coast hinterland, attending school about 20 minutes' drive from their current home.
"Our dream is to live on acreage," she said. "We spend all our time outdoors with the children, and we're craving the space to have horses, maybe some cows and veggie patches. Nothing beats the lifestyle Queensland provides for us, it's been life-changing,"
After leaving their Rose Bay apartment in late 2022, the couple landed the sprawling estate in the hills behind Burleigh Heads. Sold by owner-builder Ben Rochford, Villa Casa sits on 4497 square metres, with more than 1000 square metres of internal living space.
"I remember our first night in the house, the kids were on scooters and Bud was on his skateboard doing laps in the hallway in the kids' wing of the house. It was such a fun and joyful moment," Jesinta said.
Designed by Reece Keil Design, the property features 180-degree coastal views which, on misty days, makes the house feel like "you're floating in clouds". "Watching the sunrise over the ocean as I make the kids breakfast is a pretty special way to start the day," Jesinta said.
While the family looks forward to their next country chapter, she acknowledged Villa Casa would be difficult to top.
It features a five-bedroom main residence along with a two-bedroom guesthouse. The lime-rendered main home features double-height spaces, expansive living zones, a games room and a gourmet kitchen.
"I've been lucky enough in my career to shoot many campaigns and magazine covers at incredible homes all around the country and I can hand on heart say, I've never seen a home like this." Which is why they're planning to use the same team that built Villa Casa for their next home.
"We will engage Tidal Constructions, who built Villa Casa, to build our next project - a luxury farmhouse."
Villa Casa is slated for an August 10 auction with prestige agents Amir Mian and Justin Haynes of Amir Prestige. There is no price guide.

title: Retro uranium bans:   The AFR View
full_text:
Anthony Albanese's decision not to extend majority Rio Tinto-owned Energy Resources of Australia's lease over the undeveloped Jabiluka uranium deposit in the Northern Territory is essentially a climate war political gesture. It is aimed at Peter Dutton's equally politicised plan for a Coalition government to build seven nuclear reactors around the country, while also seeking to regain ground with Indigenous voters after last year's crushing defeat of the Voice referendum. Rio Tinto says it is pleased that the wishes of the Mirarr people to extinguish the lease have been respected. While this is the right of the native title holders, the Mirarr's fears include retro 'nuclear winter' atomic weapons proliferation that is guarded against by Australia's international treaty obligations. As Indigenous leader and nuclear company director Warren Mundine tells The Australian Financial Review today, holders of the native title that now covers much of the nation's landmass also have an opportunity to use mining as a source of jobs and economic development to help close the gap and overcome disadvantage in remote Indigenous Australia.
The Albanese government's locking up of Jabiluka forever in the Kakadu National Park comes amid a spike in global uranium demand and prices. This follows 22 countries including France, the US, UK, Japan, Canada and Sweden signing a pact at last December's UN climate summit backing a tripling of nuclear energy by 2050 to help combat climate change. By contrast, modern Labor's opposition to zero-emissions nuclear energy extends to the bans on uranium mining and sometimes exploration in NSW, Queensland, Victoria and Western Australia. When Australia is already the world's fourth-largest uranium producer and contains 30 per cent of the world's known deposits, these bans belong to a previous era's anti-nuclear environmentalism.
Given the challenge reaching net zero poses for a carbon-intensive economy whose prosperity is propped up by iron ore, coal and gas exports, Labor's efforts to keep Australia's energy transition uranium mining-free amount to a self-defeating hobbling of the nation's green superpower hopes.

title: Energy woes won't hurt green plans:   Opinion
author: Rod Sims
full_text:
The Australian Financial Review's editorial on July 3 stated that rising energy costs in Australia would undermine the federal government's Future Made in Australia strategy. This is not so.
Australia's energy market problems essentially come from seeking to move to zero emissions energy without putting a price on the negative effects of carbon emissions.
Without such a price, which Australia had from 2012-2014, the market cannot drive the transformation, and we are left with non-market based government interventions. This introduces distortions and uncertainty.
The Renewable Energy Target spurred high renewable energy investment in the late 2010s. This target stopped increasing mandatory requirements in 2020 and expires in 2030, and so no longer provides an incentive to build new renewable energy.
And when solar or wind are dominant, electricity prices fall to near zero, so the commercial incentive to build disappears.
The government has introduced the new Capacity Investment Scheme, which uses taxpayer funds to underwrite the profits of government-selected renewable energy projects.
Few, if any, investors will now build grid-connected solar or wind projects without waiting for government underwriting. Further, without a price on carbon to provide another avenue for commercial return, the scheme will be expensive to the budget.
The first round of Capacity Investment Scheme-tendered projects was heavily oversubscribed. This is as expected, since a commercial return is underwritten.
Projects that did not gain support will await the next tender; projects no longer have a market incentive to proceed otherwise.
This may compound our electricity supply shortage, which is further worsened by poor gas market policy over the last decade. Gas peaking plants can ensure sufficient 24/7 electricity supply during this interim stage of the transition.
Australian electricity costs used to be close to the world's lowest. Now they are relatively high. This is due, first, to both inadequate overall supply, and high prices for gas and coal, with these generation sources often setting the wholesale electricity price. Electricity generation makes up a third of household bills.
Second, we have excessive network costs due to our regulatory system; these make up 45 per cent of household electricity bills. While more renewable energy will eventually address the former problem, we must also tackle network costs.
While high electricity prices are a huge problem for Australia's economy and cost of living, they do not remove the outcomes expected from the Net Zero Transformation stream of the Future Made In Australia policy.
This is because many projects in the new industries can be located where they are welcomed, and away from the current grid. They will often be in the Upper Spencer Gulf, in the Pilbara, central and northern Queensland, and elsewhere in northern and remote Australia. There, Australia has an internationally recognised comparative advantage in producing green energy-intensive exports of iron, aluminium, polysilicon, fertiliser and transport fuels.
The Future Made In Australia policy supports these industries by addressing market failures that will otherwise undermine a true market-based outcome.
In particular, how can we expect green industries to compete with fossil fuel-based industries without an international carbon price that recognises the harm to the environment from carbon emissions?
Europe has an effective carbon price, and other countries will eventually have an equivalent mechanism to meet their net zero objectives as the climate science becomes even more obvious, but until then, support is needed.
Firmed renewable energy costs around $110MWh in Australia, but some big green export industries do not need 24/7 power. Intermittent renewable power costs $60-80MWh in Australia, and we have an almost endless supply of it.
The best areas are well away from rich farmland and large population centres. And there is no need for a distribution network which makes up more than a third of residential electricity costs. Away from the grid, Australia has a clear comparative advantage in low-cost energy.
Nuclear energy costs at best $200-$300MWh based on the five nuclear plants commenced since 2000 in Western economies, all of which have a history in nuclear power. Clearly, nuclear energy will not power a Future Made In Australia.
Australians are superbly placed to ride this trend by producing energy-intensive green exports which can provide way more export income than we get from coal and gas.
Let's not confuse this opportunity with the problems facing consumers drawing from the expensive east coast electricity grid.
Rod Sims is professor at the Crawford School of Public Policy and chairman of the Superpower Institute. From 2011-2022, he was chairman of the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission.

title: That cool op-shop jacket could earn you some carbon credits
author: Peter Ker
full_text:
Customers who buy second hand clothes at op-shops would earn carbon credits under a privately generated trading scheme to be considered for adoption by federal regulators.
Good Sammy Enterprises chief executive Kane Blackman said governments should offer financial incentives to people who recycle and reuse clothes in a bid to curb the greenhouse gas emissions generated by the import of new garments and textiles.
The proposal is one of 43 ideas now being assessed under the Albanese government's plan for private citizens, corporations and charities to play a bigger role in determining eligibility for Australian Carbon Credit Units (ACCUs).
Big emitters can buy an ACCU to offset one tonne of their carbon emissions, with S&P Global Platts reporting an ACCU was $34 on July 22.
The Clean Energy Regulator has devised 31 different "methods" for earning ACCU's over the past decade, but the government has this year pivoted to crowdsourcing new methods from the public, in line with the recommendations of Professor Ian Chubb's 2023 review of the ACCU scheme.
Good Sammy diverts more than 6 million kilograms of textiles from landfill each year and sells recycled clothes through its 27 retail outlets. Mr Blackman said his ACCU proposal was designed to reward actions that "avoided emissions".
"Australia is the second-highest consumer of textiles globally. Textiles produce 10 per cent of global greenhouse gas emissions. The more that is reused and processed locally in Australia reduces our global carbon emission footprint," he said.
"With 200,000 tonnes per annum of textiles being landfilled in Australia the direct carbon emissions from textiles in Australia are also significant.
"Good Sammy is interested in having the discussion on whether Australia can genuinely reduce its impact on the global carbon footprint by slowing the import of new clothing and by providing a further financial incentive for individuals and businesses opting for reuse."
The ACCU scheme already rewards some actions on the basis they "avoid" emissions; landowners in Northern Australia can earn ACCU's for conducting controlled burning of bushland - an action that releases carbon into the atmosphere - based on the notion that the controlled burns reduce the prospect of much larger, uncontrolled wildfires that would release larger amounts of carbon.
"Redirecting items from landfill, producing less stuff and lower emissions needs to be better promoted and supported," Mr Blackman said.
"There is growing recognition that there is a need to measure this recycling and reuse activity and quantify the avoided emissions.
"We believe that policies should incentivise good behaviour and we're confident that most people would be in agreement with us to keep items out of landfill, especially with the rising cost of living and increased consumerism."
Mr Blackman's proposal and the 42 others in the first round of "proponent-led" ideas were submitted to government in July and are now being assessed by the government's Emissions Reduction Assurance Committee led by Professor Karen Hussey.
The committee will recommend the best proposals to Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen, who will choose which ones to enshrine as official "methods" for earning ACCUs.
Professor Chubb's "proponent led" system was an acknowledgement technical knowledge needed for nascent carbon capture and emissions reduction technologies was more likely to exist outside government bureaucracy.

title: Eraring lifeline 'will keep bills down'
author: Angela Macdonald-Smith
full_text:
Delaying the closure of Origin Energy's huge Eraring coal power station would prevent a surge in household power bills and reduce the risk of blackouts, the NSW government was told in modelling ahead of its decision to extend the plant's life by at least two years.
Keeping the 2880-megawatt generator running past August 2025 - the date Origin was due to turn the plant off - would mean wholesale power prices would be about $55 a megawatt-hour lower in 2025-26, according to energy market forecasts provided to the state.
The difference in wholesale prices would still be significant the following year, at $40/MWh, the government was told.
"Residential bills will be impacted if Eraring retires on time," Endgame Economics - which was engaged by the NSW Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water to model the impact in the power market of delaying the closure - said in its advice.
The firm said that putting back the closure date would have "minimal" impact on private investment in the electricity sector, assuming state targets for renewables are met on time. While emissions are higher if Eraring is extended, they would not impact the achievement of NSW's 2030 emissions reduction target, it was told.
The modelling from Endgame Economics and ICA Partners the Minns Labor government relied on to clinch the deal in May with Origin to extend Eraring's operations is to be tabled in state parliament today. The release of the modelling is in line with the state government's commitment then to make it public. The agreement will cost up to $225 million a year, depending on whether Origin needs to call on it to compensate for losses at the generator.
NSW Energy Minister Penny Sharpe said the modelling was being released to show the government was being fully transparent about the decision to keep Eraring running.
"This agreement will manage an orderly exit from coal-fired power to ensure the lights stay on for homes, businesses and industry while NSW delivers the transition to low-cost, reliable renewable energy," she said, describing the agreement as "temporary and targeted".
The Australian Energy Market Operator warned last year the risk of blackouts in NSW would rise if Eraring closed in August 2025. Output at Eraring reached a five-year high in 2023-24, partly due to low wind power generation early this winter.
The risk of unreliable supplies of power in NSW if the plant closed in 2025 was the main consideration that warrants the NSW government thinking about "insurance options", ICA Partners told the state.
ICA calculated the total benefit from extending Eraring was about $4.8 billion, while the total cost was about $1.3 billion, based on Endgame's forecast of the payments under the deal.
The net economic benefit in present value terms of the Origin deal is between $3.2 billion and $3.5 billion, the department said. It put benefits at $4.4 billion in reduced wholesale electricity costs, $300 million from increased reliability of electricity, and $200 million from avoided costs of providing "system strength" services to the grid. Those benefits outweigh the $1.1 billion economic cost of increasing carbon emissions, $200 million in increased costs for the NSW electricity infrastructure road map and $400 million of potential payments to Origin.

title: Japanese giant comes calling for Smart Energy:   Street Talk
author: Sarah Thompson, Kanika Sood and Emma Rapaport
full_text:
Japanese appliance maker Rinnai Corporation, capitalised at ¥439 billion ($4.8 billion) on the Tokyo Stock Exchange, has acquired a majority stake in Byron Bay-headquartered Smart Energy, which called in KPMG to shop the business last year.
Street Talk understands Rinnai's Australian subsidiary, best known for its heating, cooling and hot water systems, will use Smart Energy as a toehold to get into Australia's market for renewable energy solutions, where 314,507 residential rooftop solar photo-voltaic systems were installed in 2023. The sector contributed 11.2 per cent of the combined national electricity production.
Smart Energy, founded in 2016 by Beau Savage and Elliot Hayes out of a Byron Bay warehouse, has worked with more than 20,000 clients, installing rooftop solar systems and accompanying batteries as well as heat pumps.
The business has 15 outlets and 300 employees, and was shopped with $50 million revenue. Of note, it has been growing the top line at 19 per cent since 2018 on a compounded annual growth basis, and is expected to hit $200 million in sales within a few years.
It's a marriage between a 104-year-old product manufacturer and a fast-growing service provider.
Smart Energy's co-founders - Hayes and Savage are joined by chief operating officer Jasper Boyschau - are teaming up with Rinnai at a time when the trio sets its sights on expanding beyond their rooftop solar roots to wedge deeper into residential users' electrification of their homes.
As an example, Smart Energy has an electricity retail licence and helps its customers to pool their batteries into third-party virtual power plants (VPPs) to allow them to sell into the grid; it is now heading towards setting up a VPP of its own.
It sees Queensland as red-hot for its battery installations business.
Hayes told Street Talk the business has a 5 per cent slice of the highly fragmented market for battery installations, where several smaller players are beginning to consolidate as they stare down the challenge of making the jump from installing subsidised solar installations to an "energy lifestyle" business.
"Our partnership with Rinnai will allow us to leverage its expertise in manufacturing and supply chain management to further enhance the quality of our products. Together, we will drive innovation, improve operational efficiencies, and create even greater value for our customers," Hayes said.
Rinnai has been in Australia for nearly 50 years, and last earned a mention in this column when it carved out ASX-listed GWA Group's air-conditioning and heating business Brivis for $49 million a decade ago.

title: Farmers cottoning on to $4.2b crop threat
author: James Hall
full_text:
The rising threat of diseases has threatened to decimate the $4.2 billion cotton industry, prompting expert groups to join forces to protect crops and the booming export market.
A $13 million partnership between the Cotton Research and Development Corporation (CRDC), University of South Queensland and the Queensland government hopes to offer a new strategy to shield growers.
Fifth-generation grower Mick Humphries, who runs cotton crops in Moree, NSW, said the collaborative approach was much-needed.
He said diseases cost his business about 20 per cent of his gross income per year and hoped a new and co-ordinated strategy would be more effective.
"The way things have worked in the past has been smaller projects and some larger projects, and they've all been run concurrently and at times the communication between those doing the research hasn't always gelled," Mr Humphries told The Australian Financial Review. "The way this project is working now, with everything being controlled from a central location, it should really give the stability to make some improvement."
Australian cotton exports soared to $4.2 billion in 2022-23 from $2.2 billion in 2021-22 as year-on-year volume figures surged nearly 70 per cent higher.
But this booming sector faces constant danger from new diseases, with climate change threatening to increase the spread.
CRDC innovation broker Elsie Hudson said the Australian Cotton Disease Collaboration (ACDC), to be launched today, aimed to reduce the economic effect of current and emerging diseases from 14 per cent to less than 5 per cent by 2028. She said the goal was to implement modern research and development methods to overhaul the approach to defending against diseases. "Disease is a critical challenge for Australia's cotton industry, contributing to significant yield losses, which undermine long-term confidence in growing cotton," Ms Hudson said.
"In extreme cases, disease pressure is forcing some growers to opt out of cotton production."
Research commissioned by the CRDC found disease is causing an 8 per cent reduction in yield while those directly affected have lost 12 per cent on average and the more extreme cases have had 100 per cent of their crops wiped out.
"Their entire crop is at risk," Ms Hudson said. "While CRDC has invested in cotton disease research over several decades, the impact disease is having on growers' profitability and productivity is increasing.
"A new approach is needed to overcome this persistent, leading limitation in the cotton production system."
UniSQ associate professor Sambasivam Periyannan, the director of the program, said the university's Toowoomba campus in Queensland was uniquely positioned to drive change.
"As a nationwide collaborative project, ACDC brings multiple experts from various agencies together to tackle disease in cotton," he said.
"Importantly, this project will look to extend beyond national borders, and collaborate with cotton researchers from leading cotton-producing countries overseas, namely, USA, India, China, Brazil, and Pakistan.
"Through knowledge and material sharing, this global network will ensure the Australian cotton industry's preparedness and contribution to the global cotton industry's resilience against outbreaks of new strains of cotton pathogens."
