title: Letters
author: None
full_text:
Amazing Nestory, family I would like to thank Michael McGuire for his heartwarming story about the young soccer player Nestory Irankunda (15/11).
To read such positive and joyful news after so much horror and grief was really uplifting.
This refugee family has totally supported their young soccer star, to the extent that his three elder brothers, who also loved to play, withdrew from the game in order to give Nestory the chance.
This was because the family could not afford the fees for all the boys to play. Reading that brought tears to my eyes.
Congratulations and best wishes to Nestory and all your family. Well done Michael.
Catherine More, Seaford
Harrap’s words Well done Bob Harrap for putting up your hand and admitting, “I was self-entitled, arrogant and I’ve had to own that”.
You did do the crime and you did do the time!
I hope many a government fat cat, politician and council CEO will read this and remember Bob’s words, especially the words self-entitled and arrogant.
Peter McDonnell, Bridgewater
Govt’s hydro support The article ‘Hydro plant pump-up’ (16/11), a government enterprise, shows how important government support is for new-developing technologies where shortsighted investors fear to tread.
Hydrogen gas is the fuel of the future and, ideally, green production processes are used.
If as reported in Labor’s hydrogen bill there is a potential for a “pathway to dirty blue hydrogen” (Greens energy spokesman Robert Simms) production, it must include a strong element of effective carbon capture and storage of greenhouse gases.
CC&S will work given the essential government support required. Along with stopping GHG emissions, with governments leading the way, universal adoption of these world-saving technologies is just over the horizon.
Phil Cornelius, Seacliff Park
Eyes an urgent priority The parlous state of eye health in South Australia has been festering for years (‘No end to eye pain’, 13/11).
In 2015 it became apparent that Transforming Health had distorted and decimated the availability of eye health services, particularly for the aged.
The impractical plan for a statewide dedicated eye hospital at Modbury was abandoned, but this accompanied the closure of the major eye (ophthalmology) centre at the Repat and the chronic inadequacy of the services at our public hospitals. The problem was amplified when the new RAH opened in 2017 with a markedly diminished ophthalmology service.
Concerned medical colleagues, along with the Royal Society for the Blind, vigorously lobbied health ministers to establish an accessible and centralised Eye Health facility. Promises were made and in 2018 some definitive actions were taken. But, nothing has happened!
This is a serious omission in health care, particularly in the elderly. It is predicted that blindness and visual impairment will increase by 20 per cent in the next five years.
This will be higher in SA, where the main cause, age-related macular degeneration, will be reflected in our ageing population.
This health issue must reclaim an urgent priority in our overstretched health and hospital system.
Professor Warren Jones AO, Malvern
Motorcycling benefits I sincerely wish to thank Dr Randal Williams (Letters, 15/11) and the many doctors, nurses and first responders that piece together motorcycle accidents.
As a motorcyclist for over 50 years, my wholehearted thanks goes out to all those involved. I try to understand his anguish as he has been in the front line.
I would like to point out the many positives of motorcycling. Many people die from all sorts of reasons, heart disease, stroke, cancer, etc, etc, the list goes on. In the same edition of Letters to the Editor I noted one contributor wrote that we have lost 60,000 men to suicide since the late 1990s.
Camaraderie and a sense of belonging to the motorcycling fraternity is powerful. I would never condone alcohol and drug abuse whilst riding and agree that full protective gear should be worn.
Motorcyclists know the risks but see the rewards as a far greater offset. Life is short so enjoy it to the fullest.
Maybe a government campaign aimed at car drivers to be more aware of motorcyclists, similar to the current cyclist education campaign, may have some effect.
Allan Ashmoore, Victor Harbor
Townhouses needed While the SA government has released more land to developers for more homes to be built they are still not doing enough.
On Anzac Hwy there is a very large piece of land which used to have Housing SA flats with hundreds of people in them.
The property is on the northern side of Anzac Hwy, west of Cromer St, Camden Park. About two thirds of these flats have been demolished and have been for sometime. The other third of these blocks of flats still exist but they are fenced off awaiting demolition.
This location could have more than 30-plus townhouses built there but it sits idle and it’s hard to understand why. David Bishop, South Plympton

title: Something’s frosty in state of Denmark
author: Tiffany Bakker
full_text:
Crown Prince Frederik and Crown Princess Mary have appeared together for their first solo engagement amid the fallout of a furious affair denial by a glamorous socialite.
The Danish royal couple have carried out engagements with other family members, as well as the King and Queen of Spain, but this was their first public appearance as a couple, since the scandal of Prince Frederik’s night out in Madrid with Mexican socialite Genoveva Casanova.
It comes as a body language expert declared there was apparent “tension” between the couple in the official photos shared by Copenhagen’s Royal Palace.
Body language expert Judi James claimed Princess Mary’s rigid stance suggests there is “tension”, while her pursed lips “hint at judgmental thinking”. As for Prince Frederik, James told the Daily Mail that his crossed arms add to the “air of coolness” in the room, even though he looked more relaxed.
The royal palace shared pictures of the royals with Denmark’s climate ambassador Tomas Anker Christensen at Amalienborg Palace, Copenhagen, to Instagram on Thursday local time.
The pair met with Mr Christensen to discuss Denmark’s climate efforts ahead of COP28 in Dubai in December.
subject: Queens

title: Wind and solar ‘will destroy a third of our farm land’
author: James Morrow
full_text:
Australia could lose one-third of its productive agricultural land to solar panels and wind farms if the government pushes forward with its plans to reach net-zero emissions entirely through wind and solar, a new study has warned.
The alert comes as the ­Coalition signalled a new push to remove bans on uranium mining and exploration, as well as the ban on nuclear power plants, which have a much smaller footprint that solar and wind farms.
According to analysis by the Institute of Public Affairs, Australia produced about 5000 terawatt-hours of energy from oil, gas and coal in 2023.
Due to growing energy demand in Australia and among our trading partners, the amount of energy that represents would increase to more than 15,000 terawatt-hours by 2050. And to meet the demand, and become a “renewable energy superpower”, replacing that power with a 50-50 mix of wind and solar would require 119 million hectares of land – an amount equal to 15 per cent of the country’s landmass and a third of all agricultural land.
The study notes that modelling by Net Zero Australia has already said “five Tasmanias worth of solar farms will be needed to produce the energy necessary to replace Australia’s current hydrocarbon fuel exports in addition to domestic consumption”.
By contrast, nuclear power is very “dense”, requiring far less land to generate an equivalent amount of electricity.
At the COP28 Climate Summit in Dubai last week, more than two dozen nations led by the US pledged to triple nuclear power generation capacity to help meet net-zero targets by 2050. Opposition energy spokesman Ted O’Brien on Saturday urged Australia to remove restrictions on nuclear power. “It’s time we took back energy security for the West, and we should do so ambitiously for we have the capacity as a nation to do more than just supply uranium but also develop capabilities in other areas of the nuclear fuel cycle,” he said.

Public deserves apology Terry Hewton spoke too soon in supporting federal Attorney-Gerneral Mark Dreyfus’s castigation of a reporter who had asked him to apologise to the people of Australia (Letters, 8/12).
The Advertiser reported in the same edition that Mr Dreyfus has privately apologised to the journalist for his verbal attack.
The Prime Minister said publicly that it had breached parliamentary standards, and Foreign Minister Penny Wong said Dreyfus might later regret his words (Dreyfus sorry for detainee saga outburst, 8/12).
Dreyfus should have apologised to the people of Australia – not for obeying the High Court, but for failing to plan in advance for its likely ruling on indefinite detention.
Moreover, he could have waited for publication of the High Court’s reasons before he set about releasing potentially dangerous criminals.
Lindsay Dent, Campbelltown
Labor failing at task David Harris (Letters, 8/12) is correct in most of his letter about the ambulance ramping issue and I agree, it does seem both almost universal and insoluble.
However, he misses the main point and major irritant for most people. At the last election, the Labor Party and its union fellows campaigned almost exclusively on the promise to fix ramping.
There may be many interpretations of those words, but the current situation does not appear among them.
Where is Ash when we need her? Not to mention the apparent shortage of chalk to decorate ambulances.
Paul Buxton, Westbourne Park
Check your speed To Mike Howard of Goolwa North (Letters, 8/12), can I suggest that to avoid being tailgated at 110km/h you might need to check your actual speed with a simple GPS app on your phone which can be had for free.
My 8-year-old vehicle with brand new tyres needs to be driven at 118km/h reading on the speedometer to actually be doing the open speed limit.
It takes two minutes to check your actual speed.
This may alleviate this problem, but unfortunately it won’t stop the idiots who drive badly.
Rob Whittaker, Semaphore South
Time to be alarmed I refer to the letter by Mary-Anne Higgins (Spurrier’s claim, 8/12). I’m alarmed that such beliefs persist in ignoring overwhelming evidence from huge numbers of the world’s leading experts.
Covid-19 and climate change are things to be alarmed about Ms Higgins. Climate change deniers are living in another world, not ours. Developing and existing technologies in renewables etc. for a liveable future are well in progress and are hampered by agencies clinging to their greenhouse gasses profitmaking enterprises.
The forward-looking, environmentally caring entrepreneurs and civilisation-conscious leaders will be the ultimate profit winners.
Phil Cornelius, Seacliff Park
Seaweed not appealing I read the article (New seaweed research facility, 5/12) but there were no reasons provided for the need for such research.
So I went online and found that one line of research was food for commercial consumption by people.
People eating seaweed is not new, but it is not widespread.
However, given the climate alarmists push for less meat and dairy consumption by people, is this just a step to achieve these goals?
Are we heading towards the movie Soylent Green?
P. Quartuccio, Lockleys
Parents must have choice Caleb Bond blames “guff and activism” in the syllabus for the recent slide in school performance in Australia (Need to get back to basics in the classroom, 8/12).
His concern is justified, but is not the whole story.
There is a deeper problem underlying the chaos and misbehaviour that now erupts in too many classrooms, making teaching and learning so much more difficult.
It was predicted by studies comparing very young children who spend more than 20 hours a week in childcare centres with those raised by a loving family member.
The former suffer more stress and become more aggressive and defiant – traits that continue into school years, affecting their own learning and that of others.
More teacher pay will not solve this crisis.
Giving parents the choice to spend government childcare support on outsourced care or their own home care would be a step in the right direction.
Roslyn Phillips, Tea Tree Gully
Support missing Recently the Environment Minister Tanya Plibersek announced the federal government decision to honour the agreement to South Australia and return 450GL to the environment along with its long-term sustainability.
Where is the required support from leading Liberal SA federal members of parliament Anne Ruxton and Simon Birmingham?
Birmingham joined in the parliamentary circus with television appearances last week over the decision by the High Court of Australia to release the refugees held in indefinite detention, yet remained silent over his state’s long awaited success over the Murray and Coorong. title: If only those Teal voters had listened to me
author: Joe Hildebrand
full_text:
The left love to talk. Better still, they love to shout. What they can’t seem to do – despite constantly demanding it of others – is listen.
But who could have predicted this catastrophic collapse in the blue-collar vote for what is supposed to be the blue collar party? Why weren’t we told?!?
Many of the ultra-rich luvvies probably just didn’t care and still don’t. They wanted to register their right-side-of-history votes on issues like climate change, but of course couldn’t bring themselves to dirty their names by voting Labor.

But the perennially shocked and outraged left will pretend that this was a wholly unforeseen event caused by circumstances entirely beyond their control or a sinister conspiracy of right-wing capitalist forces.

Making the grade Just saw my second post in a fortnight on Facebook (two unrelated individuals posting). Both postings were of childcare “graduations”! Not uni, high school, or even primary school, where someone actually needs to prove their worthiness to graduate.
No, these young children had “graduated” from childcare. Hats, gowns, “diplomas”, for everyone.
Please, this is a joke, isn’t it? – “graduating” from an institution that one attends simply because the parents can’t look after a child during working hours?
We are not America, but the way our children are being brought up, it is only a matter of time before we embrace all things US.
The next generation won’t know anything different.
Richard Nelson, Modbury North Ask the alumni I have been wondering why the alumni of the University of Adelaide were not polled as to their feelings on this apparently done deal to merge our top university with our lowest ranking university, UniSA.
I graduated in 1979 with Bachelors of Medicine and Surgery.
Adelaide University still held a rank of 88 in the world universities this year. UniSA was ranked between 310-350. So why merge two very different universities with different courses to make one massive university which will now be lucky to be ranked in the top 300 worldwide?
It is a political idea, to get in yet more overseas students, who we are told like these massive universities, and something we are now trying to cut back due to misuse of student visas and enormous immigration in the midst of a housing crisis. I very much doubt that the students think this mega uni is a great idea. Did anyone ask them?
Students go from schools of 1300 or fewer students to a university of about 10,000 students. It is a massive culture shock. But it is even worse if you become one of 25,000 students. People become numbers. Campuses lose their feel of being special.
Why is this being done at such expense when we are told no jobs will be lost? It is because the government gets to sell open spaces used by universities for sports for housing estates.
Where are all those students going to be able to play sports now? We were not asked. The merger was already under way before it was announced. Why weren’t we asked? It’s all about money and taking university land away from the people who use it, it helps balance the budget. But a lot of people are not happy about it.
This government is determined to have the new WCH at the heritage Thebarton Police Barracks despite the enormous expense in relocating those units. The new WCH could have been built in a number of other places without having to also relocate the police horse and dog squads. What’s a $100m to this government? They decided and despite the outrage that has been caused will not back down.
We need to hold our politicians accountable for what they are doing and the incredible waste of money on pet projects.
Making big decisions without public consultation is not on.
Dr Patricia R M Betros, Myrtle Bank Seeing our game Surely the programming department at Channel 7 must have been on the Christmas cheer early. Why last Friday’s Big Bash game between the Adelaide Strikers and the Sydney Sixers wasn’t on free-to-air is hard to fathom.
Instead was a 90-minute Better Homes and Gardens.
Only a few days earlier, Channel 7 covered the Perth Scorchers-Hobart Hurricanes match.
I would say most cricket viewers in Adelaide couldn’t give a rats about that game, which was very one-sided.
Bob Cowley, Broadview Ageless comedy As I progressed through Nicolle Flint’s analysis of the movie Love Actually, I realised that she was actually serious (“Christmas fave should be ‘Sexism , Actually’”, The Advertiser, 22/12).
It was disturbing to read her sad interpretation of this endearing, ageless comedy. The binary gender characteristics so cleverly displayed in this uplifting film had nothing to do with the darker side of sexism.
Warren Jones, Malvern Nuclear’s OK for subs Having just watched a TV show about nuclear power throughout the world and the safety of it, from many qualified people, I am concerned about climate change and yes, I do have solar panels.
The governments of Australia, both federal and state, are condoning it by stealth. Yes they receive mining royalties from uranium mines which export it overseas – it seems to be good for them to power another countries but not ours.
We are assisting other countries to reduce their pollution but not ours. It is about time we had a good look at nuclear power –after all we will have our navy with nuclear submarines on order. It’s a bit hypocritical, I think.
There seems to be no knowledge of the differing pronunciations of verbs and nouns.
For example the word “survey” when used as a noun is pronounced “SUR-vey” but as a verb is “sur-VEY”. And don’t get me started on the stress put on “re” in such words as “research”, together with many others.
Bill Mudie, Flagstaff Hill Bans won’t work Like much of the population, Eugen mistakenly thinks that we can police stupid drivers by banning them from driving for life (Text Talk, The Advertiser, 26/12).
When will we wake up to the reality that there is a significant number of those among us who are simply defiant of the law and continue to drive while disqualified?
Nothing will change until the judges get into the real world and start showing some backbone by jailing the idiots who have no compunction in exposing their fellow citizens to the risk of injury or death on our roads. Geoff Forbes, Kensington Gardens

title: Coalition MPs meet to approve nuclear locations
author: Clare Armstrong
full_text:
The Coalition will unveil proposed locations for nuclear power plants, after a flurry of final meetings to lock in its long-awaited energy policy.
The opposition shadow cabinet were expected Tuesday night to agree on the specific retiring or former coal-fired power station sites where nuclear reactors were preferred to be built, before the proposal was to be presented to the industry, energy and resources backbench committee for consideration.
Following that discussion, it is understood Coalition MPs with electorates identified as the host locations for future nuclear reactors would be briefed on the plan.
The draft policy was to be taken to a full partyroom meeting scheduled to be held virtually at 8.30am Wednesday.
Multiple Coalition MPs said they believed the nuclear plan would be unveiled by Opposition Leader Peter Dutton later Wednesday.
However, a further “strategy” meeting had been floated as a possibility before the official announcement was made.
One Coalition MP said there was a strong feeling in the ­partyroom that Mr Dutton should capitalise on recent ­political momentum fuelled by doubts cast on Labor’s ability to achieve its target of a 43 per cent emissions cut by 2030.
However, not everyone in the partyroom was convinced about the timing, with several MPs privately saying they felt it was a risk to announce ahead of a parliamentary sitting fortnight later this month where they would be open to government attack.
There are four coal power stations in NSW, eight in Queensland, three in Victoria and three in Western Australia, which all have potential to be the sites for reactors.
In order for this to happen, a future Coalition government would have to lift Australia’s longstanding moratorium on onshore nuclear development. A CSIRO report estimated it would take until the 2040s for the first nuclear reactor to be built, which the scientific body costed at $8.5bn. Mr Dutton dismissed the figures.

title: Nuclear reaction to Budget
author: Paul Starick
full_text:
A GP payroll tax grab would be axed and a royal commission into nuclear energy ordered under a Liberal government, Opposition Leader David Speirs has vowed.
Delivering his budget reply speech on Tuesday morning, Mr Speirs accused Labor of raising the cost of visiting a doctor during a cost-of-living crisis by imposing the payroll tax.
He said AUKUS nuclear-powered submarine construction in Adelaide meant nuclear electricity generation should be considered in South Australia.
“The typical South Australian family is more than $20,000 worse off per year under Labor, as the cost of everyday essentials continue to soar.” Mr Speirs said the $20,000 figure was calculated by a combination of higher interest rates, energy bills, groceries, fuel and other essentials.
He said the Liberals would abolish the GP payroll tax if elected in 2026, saying this would stop sick people “paying more to see their doctor or avoiding their GP and ending up in our overwhelmed EDs”.
Mr Speirs, who last week visited AUKUS submarine nuclear reactor builder Rolls-Royce’s plant in Derby, UK, said a royal commission would consider the viability of nuclear energy generation in SA.
“I’ve long been saying we need to have an open-minded conversation about the potential for a civil nuclear industry in South Australia, as we’re paying some of the highest electricity prices in the world and every option to produce affordable, reliable power should be on the table,” he said. Treasurer Stephen Mullighan demanded Mr Speirs declare whether he would cut services or raise taxes to fund his promises.
“Today David Speirs committed a future Liberal government to spending hundreds and hundreds of millions of dollars more, and at the same time committed to tackling the state’s debt levels,” he said.
“There’s only two options he has to achieve this, and one is to massively cut the services that South Australians rely on from tje state government or to increase taxes.
“And now he must tell South Australians which one of those he will deliver, should he be premier.” A landmark court ruling last year found GPs working in clinics as contractors are deemed employees — making such clinics liable for payroll tax. The government granted an amnesty on the tax but will start charging from July 1. It says it is not a new tax, just correct application of an existing tax.

title: BHP’s electric dreams need Pilbara renewables
author: Cameron England
full_text:
BHP will source 500MW of renewable power and storage in the Pilbara by 2030 and have its first all-electric truck fleet operational before the end of the decade, under its plans to achieve its 30 per cent emissions reduction target.
The global miner is also working on technology advancements on the steelmaking front, and sees carbon capture and storage and a move to more electricity-powered steelmaking as providing the major abatement benefits in that sector.
BHP’s vice-president for climate Dr Graham Winkelman said the company was likely to report “a small increase” in operational emissions this financial year, with that understood to be largely down to growth in production.
The global miner said on Wednesday it was on track to deliver “at least” a 30 per cent reduction in scope one and two greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 against a 2020 baseline, and maintained its aspirational target to be net zero by 2050.
Dr Winkelman said the company had made good progress on the power front through the use of power purchase agreements.
Diesel is now the largest source of emissions across BHP, with Dr Winkelman saying on Wednesday the company had determined that electrifying its truck and train fleets and powering the fleets with renewable energy was the best path forward.
In the Pilbara iron ore region in northern Western Australia, BHP is unable to take advantage of power purchase agreements to buy renewable energy as the area is off the main grid.
Therefore, BHP was looking at how to source renewable energy, BHP vice-president of operation decarbonisation Dan Heal said.
“In Western Australia Iron Ore, our inland Pilbara operations are not connected to an existing grid and so we cannot purchase power through the market,’’ Mr Heal said.
“Renewable technologies such as wind and solar are available, but the Pilbara is remote, so we are working through the best way to introduce large volumes of renewable energy, or other sources of low to zero emissions power, while keeping power running 24/7, 365 days a year.
“By the end of this decade, we plan to have up to 500MW of wind, solar and battery storage assets available in the Pilbara.
“We also expect significant demand growth to occur post FY2030, with diesel displacement increasing the amount of electricity required at some of our operated assets by up to four times. “This means securing a reliable supply of renewable and other low to zero emission energy into the future remains a significant priority.’’
subject: Alternative energy sources; Emissions; Iron compounds; Renewable resources

title: OLIVER’S ARMY
author: Story MICHAEL McGUIRE
full_text:
OLIVER DOUGLAS IS ONLY 23. A RHODES SCHOLAR, HE WILL MOVE TO OXFORD UNIVERSITY THIS YEAR. AFTER THAT’S HE’S NOT SURE. ACADEMIC. SOLDIER. MAYBE EVEN A FUTURE LEADER OF THE LIBERAL PARTY Oliver Douglas wants to restore faith in democracy. No easy feat at this point in time when trust in politicians and political institutions have arguably never been at a lower ebb.
Douglas is only 23 and has some of that idealism of youth about him, but he’s also managed to pack a lot into his short life and it would be more than unfair to call him naive. He won a series of scholarships and prizes at school and university, held a world tennis ranking, is a lieutenant in the Australian Army. Has launched an app with brother Patrick. And is also now a Rhodes scholar. He has also been tipped as a future leader of the Liberal Party.
“I think one of the things that I find concerning as a young individual is trust in government is generally at record lows,’’ he says. “And yet we live in a time where we’re facing enormous complex challenges, climate crisis, wealth inequality, national security, geopolitical instability in our in our region.
“It’s probably not a great place to be in where you’ve got huge problems that require significant political will, or political action, government action, and we have record low faith in those institutions.’’ Douglas is a member of the Young Liberals and describes himself as a “classic Liberal”. He is worried that the extremes on both sides of politics have hijacked public debate.
“The voices on the extremes of our political spectrum, because they’re so vocal, they dominate that discourse, where we need people in the centre, voices who are considered and moderate to speak a bit more clearly about the value proposition that they’re offering.’’ But he has also found trying to combat those voices can be difficult. “I’ve articulated my views for where I think the party in South Australia broadly should be headed,’’ he says. “People don’t always agree with the vision that I’m offering. I think there’s a lot of people getting swept up in the broader forces of the moment and to challenge the forces of populism and things like that today is not an easy thing to do.’’ The crisis Douglas sees in modern Australian democracy is something he will examine as part of his Rhodes scholarship at Oxford. But he is going to do it by looking backwards, to see what lessons can be learnt from the past and applied to modern life.
In particular, Douglas is looking at British history from 1850 onwards to see what challenges democracy has faced since that time and how it coped. The idea being that as Australia has taken its political institutions from Britain, there could be much to learn. His broader goal being to find ways to strengthen democratic institutions.
It’s also a bit of a homecoming for Douglas, who was born in London. The Douglas family moved to Australia in 2005, when father Andrew who was a policeman in England moved as part of an SA Police recruitment program. Andrew Douglas had also been in the Royal Marines, including serving in Croatia as part of a NATO-peacekeeping force, before joining the police. He now works in the Australian Taxation Office.
His mother, Albertina, was born behind the Iron Curtain in what was still called Czechoslovakia. His mother’s stories of growing up under a Communist regime, he says, gave him a “grounding’’ and informed his own political views. Albertina, who works in a pharmacy in Seacombe Gardens, took part in the Velvet Revolution in Czechoslovakia in November and December 1989, which brought down the Communist government that had ruled for more than 40 years.
“She was born in 1973 and so lived through the latter half of that and raised me passing on some fascinating stories about state censorship control, curtailed civil liberties and things like that,’’ he says.
Or even how his mother’s family found out about the 1986 Chernobyl nuclear disaster, which was only about 1000km away, not from local authorities but from foreign media.
“The first they heard about was Swedish Free Radio going, ‘Oh, there is sort of a radioactive cloud, going across Eastern Europe’.’’ After the fall of Communism, Douglas’ mother moved to England, speaking none of the language, and met his father when she was managing a Spanish restaurant in London.
In Adelaide, the family settled in Coromandel Valley and Douglas remembers an “idyllic’’ childhood, playing cricket and tennis and living an Adelaide Hills’ kind of life. He attended Coromandel Valley Primary School, then won a scholarship to St John’s Grammar in Belair.
But it wasn’t a childhood without its setbacks. Douglas estimates between the ages of five and 15 he was operated on around 30 times at the Women’s and Children’s Hospital. In one year at primary school, he missed 80 days of school.
Douglas won’t go into detail about the nature of the problem, only saying he was battling a “recurring medical issue’’.
“I will never forget long days spent in agonising pain, my parents’ distraught faces, and that distinct sterile hospital smell – a smell I hate to this day.” He says the memories of his younger self serves as a “source of inspiration’’. “It asks me to use those painful memories both as a motivator to live a full life and to remain compassionate with others – our struggles are not always immediately clear.’’ On the bright side, missing all that school meant he also had to develop other skills.
“One of the sort of by products of always having to catch up on schoolwork is that I always from a young age had to be very organised and diligent in that sense. And I think that’s the sort of hangover effect that’s sort of maintained my latter life.’’ It was also a time that saw Douglas download a “million documentaries’’ and nourished a love of history that will carry him all the way to Oxford University later this year.
After school he decided to take a gap year to pursue another love. Tennis. He worked with Thanasi Kokkinakis’ coach Todd Langman and was ranked as the best under-18 player in SA and the 55th best player in Australia. But that was as far as it went. In the end, he says, it wasn’t that difficult to give up the dream.
“And sort of I got to the point where it’s as good as I’ll ever be,’’ he says. “And to improve further would mean giving up almost every other part of his life.
“If you wanted to be a full time sort of tennis player, I’d have to be training day in, day out. And maybe I could have done my uni studies at the same time, but I wouldn’t have been able to do them as well. I wouldn’t have been able to get involved with sort of university life and things like that,’’ he says.
Douglas’ original plan was to go to Australian National University in Canberra and study law and commerce but decided to stay at home. He won a scholarship at St Mark’s in the city and decided to study law and arts at Adelaide University. His arrival at St Mark’s coincided with the Covid-19 pandemic and all that followed. While many students left, he remained in the college, although social distancing was still in force. It meant that for late-night movie viewing, there had to be some careful seating arrangements. Douglas being a stickler for rules, was keen to comply. So while two people would sit inside the TV room “you’d have two people in the hallway watching the TV through the through the door to adhere to the 1.5m rule”.
Douglas’ uni plan also changed. While he loved the history aspects of his arts degree, he struggled to muster similar enthusiasm for law.
“It just wasn’t resonating with me the same way,’’ he says. “I felt like I was being intellectually exercised in a way that I really enjoyed in my history studies, that law was partly there, but I just didn’t quite fall in love with it in the same way.’’ By his fourth year at uni he had dropped law and undertook honours in history. He decided to do a thesis on the Howard government’s decision to build the Christmas Island detention centre. As a migrant himself, Douglas had taken subjects which looked at Australia’s migrant history. He had examined Federation in 1901 and the unwinding of the White Australia policy in the 1970s. In part, it was because he wanted to better understand the country he now called home, but also he wanted to understand how decisions are made within government.
It’s a theme he will continue to develop at Oxford University, intertwined with that desire to understand what is happening to democracies in the western world.
“I’m a huge believer that humanities has utility in terms of generating better decision makers, understanding the context of the past and things that we need to solve some of the problems that we face,’’ he says.
Douglas will be at Oxford for three years. Beyond that he is still unsure what will be his life course. There is a chance he will remain in academia, and is planning to write a book that will emerge from his Oxford study.
Another option is to remain in the military. Douglas has been serving as a full-time lieutenant in the first armoured regiment for the last six months, participating in battle exercises in places such as Cultana near Whyalla in the north of SA.
Then, of course, there is politics. At least one senior Liberal has called Douglas the “hope of the side’’. But that is no guarantee of progress. Douglas’ description of himself as a “classic Liberal’’ translates into a belief that individuals can make the world a better place. He believes in the value of institutions whether that be parliament, churches or courts. In classic Liberal style he believes in government, but only up to a point.
“You need government to assist and set parameters. But government just physically can’t do everything, ’’ he says. And nor would it be healthy if it could.
“If you have a very large government apparatus then the risk is that any government of the day can use that apparatus to enforce their will on people,’’ he says.
Douglas’ problem could be in finding a spot in the current Liberal Party, which is drifting towards an ever more conservative stance on many issues and is dominated in South Australia by its right faction.
Douglas says having his voice heard is becoming increasingly difficult. “We should live in a time of society that accepts a whole range of views and a range of things but frankly that’s an idea that seems not to be the flavour of the month on either end of politics,’’ he says.
Douglas hesitates when asked about current political leaders he admires. Instead he delves back into history and mentions names such as Australia’s longest-serving Prime Minister Robert Menzies and assassinated US President John F. Kennedy.
Another name mentioned is Charles Hawker, who was a minister in the government of Joe Lyons in the early 1930s. Hawker was born near Clare and was severely wounded in WWI. Hawker quit the Cabinet when the government would not reduce the salary of MPs during the Great Depression. Douglas’ scholarship that allowed him to attend St Mark’s was named after Hawker. “The sort of following that he still enjoys today is a product of his integrity, moral courage and doing what’s right,’’ Douglas says. “And I think that if we saw politicians taking those sorts of actions today – how much more trust do you think people would have in the system?’’ ■

title: IT'S A LATTE OF EXPENSE TO ESPRESS YOURSELF
author: Emily Macdonald
full_text:
A storm is brewing in the world of coffee with prices creeping up everywhere from your local cafe to the supermarket shelves.
Climate change, pirates, international red tape, supply problems … between the complexity of the issues and the lack of caffeine, it’s enough to give you a headache.
Rising temperatures and water shortages are playing havoc in the world’s coffee belt – located 25 degrees north and south of the equator – with countries from Brazil and Colombia to Ethiopia and Indonesia reporting declines in their harvests.
Even the hardiest robusta varieties are suffering, with Vietnamese growers telling Bloomberg they are having to dig deeper and deeper to access their once plentiful water supply.
Meanwhile in the Red Sea, the Yemeni Shia Islamist military and political group the Houthis are attacking civilian cargo ships, including many bearing coffee beans, in acts of aggression the US condemns as piracy.
As a result, freight costs have jumped 150 per cent and many countries are scrambling to find alternative suppliers.
This all comes as the EU moves to outlaw sales of coffee by December if the growers are linked to deforestation.
In the short term there are concerns the new EU regulations could exacerbate the shortages.
According to The Conversation, the average cost of a small flat white in the Australian capitals is now $4.78, while the equivalent brew sets you back $6.96 in London, $8.42 in Singapore and $9.95 in Athens.
Lavazza Group chairman Giuseppe Lavazza recently told the Financial Times prices would only get higher.
“The coffee supply chain is dramatically under pressure,” Mr Lavazza said. “Coffee prices are not going down … (they’re) going to stay very high.” While many home workers have invested in their own barista-style machines, new figures from Coles reveal sales of coffee sachets and coffee pods have increased significantly in the past year.
While instant coffee remains the least expensive way to get a caffeine hit, at nine cents a cup your average sachet costs 41 cents and coffee pod just 52 cents.
But if you appreciate the art of an expert, you cannot beat the standards set by the Australian baristas and coffee kings who are bringing our cafe culture to Americans.
Day For It Hospitality chief executive Michael Meates, who has had caffeine running through his veins for 20 years since his first job at Bacino Bar on Manly’s Corso in Sydney at age 15, said Australian coffee and cafe knowledge was particularly prized in New York City.
“America was stuck in that diner culture for a long time,” he said. “It was that 20oz (590ml) from Dunkin’ Donuts mass consumerism.
“Since the Australians came along with their flat white, and I know we can’t take full credit as we are inspired by the beautiful quality of Italian espressos, it has really elevated things here in New York.
“It’s not so much a splurge anymore. In Midtown (Manhattan) they don’t blink at $7 for a coffee. We see interns, some of them would only be getting paid $45,000, so it’s a lot of money for them, but it’s a status symbol they see their colleagues getting and they want a quality product.
“I find coffee is very much like the wine industry. Sommeliers have been able to explain this to people for some time.
“Yeah you can get a coffee for $3 but it’s not going to taste that good.” Partner Coffee Roasters is another Aussie beverage success story, with co-owners Amber Jacobsen and Adam Boyd adding to their trio of NYC cafes and presence in Whole Foods outlets with a flourishing trade in home coffee.
The brand has quickly developed a cult following, with subscribers receiving monthly bags of beans and cold brew syrup.
Partners Coffee Green Bean buyer Sam Klein said the cost of a coffee was going up because expenses were increasing across the board, from commercial leases and packaging to transportation.
But the industry was also keeping coffee lovers hooked with new blends. “I’ve seen some really exciting signature drinks lately incorporating interesting flavour combinations,” he said. “We’ve recently had a Yuzu Vanilla Latte and a Black Sesame Cold Brew, which our director of coffee, Cary, developed, that were really fun,” he said.
“And we’ve done some cool experiments recently with szechuan peppercorns to make some really refreshing tonics. I’ve seen a lot of other cafes doing similar things, and the results are often texturally really interesting, too. If I could manifest a trend, I’d like to see more attention to exceptional batch brew, especially using single origin and single variety coffees.” Mr Klein said the company had “found success in at-home channels” but “it comes with its own set of challenges” for the business.
“I don’t get to come into your home and taste your coffee or spread my enthusiasm for a producer or variety in person,” he said.
“But it’s been a lot of fun for me because it has increased demand.” Tony Oxdale, from Sydney, now resides on Balboa Island in Newport Beach, California, and has two coffee ventures – Drop Bear Coffee for roasting, packaging and shipping, and Il Caccia, which boasts two mobile espresso bars.
Mr Oxdale said despite price hikes, and a worldwide shortage of Papua New Guinea beans (one of the main blend components) they were growing in a most competitive market.
“We can provide all types of coffee types from whole bean, ground to suit your brew method and even K cups,” he said.
“I know most Australians complain about the standard of coffee here, and I am trying to satisfy that need.”

title: With hydrogen, SA will be in its element with net zero
author: Alexander Downer
full_text:
I’m an investor in two low-carbon energy sources in South Australia. One is a solar farm in the Mid North. It’s a nice project and will probably make a modest return on my investment.
The other is a groundbreaking project to obtain natural hydrogen from under the Yorke Peninsula and Kangaroo Island. Now that is a really exciting project.
Back in the Great Depression, a group of Yorke Peninsula and Kangaroo Island farmers – in desperation – hired a drilling company to look for oil and gas. They didn’t find any. All they found was hydrogen and, as there was no market for it in the 1930s, the project was abandoned.
Today, there is a market for hydrogen as a zero-emission energy source. It can be used in the transport sector, ammonia production and, importantly, steel production.
SA is blessed with it. It’s estimated there are 1.3 billion kilograms of natural hydrogen in the Yorke Peninsula. That’s a lot of hydrogen which could make a sizeable contribution to the heroic political goal of net zero by 2050. What’s more, hydrogen could be exported, particularly to Japan. So, make no mistake, hydrogen could be a sizeable income earner for the state if the economics can be made to work.
It’s the economics of energy, which explains why there’s such heated debate about climate-change policies.
The popular method of obtaining commercial hydrogen is to produce it by electrolysis. If the requisite electricity were produced by a gas-fired power station, the cost of the hydrogen would be about $5.60 a kilogram. To keep emissions down, the plan is to use renewables to produce the necessary electricity. That’s what’s called green hydrogen. To produce that would cost an estimated $6 a kilogram.
Green hydrogen projects do sound good. That’s why the SA government is working on a $600m investment in a hydrogen production power station and storage facility in Whyalla.
But short of substantial government subsidies, there is a question about whether green hydrogen is a long-term solution.
Natural hydrogen just drilled from the ground is a different story. This is an industry in its infancy, and SA is one of the most prospective natural hydrogen sources on Earth. Assuming a satisfactory flow rate, natural hydrogen from the peninsula could be extracted at a cost of about $1 a kilogram.
For economic activity to be sustainable and to contribute to economic growth, it has to be profitable. Even governments of the most feckless variety won’t continue to pour your money into loss-making enterprises. The more they do, the poorer it makes us all. But if we can couple green sustainable energy with positive returns for investors – and over a long period of time – then we might be on to something big.

title: Economy on the edge, testing times are ahead
author: None
full_text:
Stockmarkets across the world have plunged and the global economy is on the precipice.
Monday was a bloodbath for the Australian market, with more than $100bn wiped off its value as the S&P/ASX 200 index sunk by 3.7 per cent.
Investors have been spooked by fears the US economy is headed for recession. These fears have been stoked by unexpectedly weak employment and manufacturing data.
The consequences of the world’s largest economy sinking into recession are far-reaching, not least for Australia.
Initially, the Reserve Bank should start setting a course for interest rate cuts, even if one is not announced on Tuesday afternoon, following the lead of the Bank of England last week and an anticipated cut by the US Federal Reserve in September.
Fledgling Reserve Bank Governor Michele Bullock must not repeat the mistakes of her predecessor Philip Lowe, whose reign was tarnished by making the wrong move at the wrong time. He disastrously signalled, as late as 2021, that historically low interest rates would not rise again “until at least 2024”.
For some time, there have been warnings that an economic winter is coming. Australian businesses and households are already heaving under the weight of successive interest rate blows. But the Albanese government has been ambushed by the cost-of-living crisis and, months away from the next federal election, has done little to stop the bleeding.
Prices of petrol, groceries and energy, in particular, remain painfully high. Labor condemns nuclear energy as unaffordable yet ploughs billions into a renewable energy transformation that is, at best, uncertain in terms of cost and effectiveness.
The savage pain of mass unemployment and elevated interest rates in the early-1990s recession is unknown to most Australians – only those of middle age and older remember that dreadful time as adults.
Debt has ballooned at state and federal levels, leaving governments comparably short of cash to splash – like they did in response to the 2008 global financial crisis and the Covid-19 pandemic.
There are testing times ahead, regardless of whether the US or Australia sink into recession.
On the evidence thus far, the Albanese government is not up to the challenge. Responsibility for all editorial comment is taken by The Editor, Gemma Jones, 31 Waymouth St, Adelaide, SA, 5000

title: We can iron out the issues with carbon
author: Cameron England
full_text:
Magnetite Mines says Australia should create a green iron centre of excellence and set a goal of producing at least 10 million tonnes of export-quality green iron by 2035.
In the company’s submission to the federal government’s green metals con-sultation paper, it argues that the absence of domestic facilities to test and demonstrate the production of Australian green iron was a significant barrier to getting the industry going.
Chief executive Tim Dobson says the global industry has a “carbon problem’’ that the emerging Australian green steel sector can help address.
“However, we are not the only nation eyeing this opportunity, and Australia must act now to seize the opportunity to produce green iron if it is to secure the massive economic, environmental and regional community benefits possible by being a first-mover in this industry,’’ Mr Dobson said.
Magnetite Mines is working to develop its Razorback iron ore project in eastern South Australia, where it has a resource of six billion tonnes of magnetite ore.
“The Razorback Iron Ore Project will produce high-value direct reduction-grade concentrates, suitable for green iron production, and is set to become a very long-life project with expansion optionality in a tier-one jurisdiction that will produce a superior iron ore product sought by steelmakers globally,’’ the company says.
“Magnetite Mines’s primary recommendation for the consultation paper is that Australia must act soon because time is running out.
Secondly, the company envisages production starting “in the form of an expandable-scale green iron facility with the support of national and state government policies and infrastructure support’’.
The third step was to scale up, aiming for 5Mtpa of green iron by 2030 and 10Mtpa by 2035. Magnetite Mines says using the hydrogen produced from that also emerging sector, produced using renewable energy, would enable the production of direct reduced iron or hot-briquetted iron for export. Such a product “is forecast to be in increasingly high demand by our key trading partners, including Japan, Korea and Taiwan, but also by China, India and other steel producing Asian countries’’, the company says.
“Each of these countries and their steelmakers have made decarbonisation commitments and are actively seeking green iron supply chains to help meet those commitments. “By 2030, demand for DR-grade pellets is expected to reach between 80-100 million tonnes per year.”

title: Letters
full_text:
Same old story
High inflation? Rising prices? Solution? Use monetary policy via the Reserve Bank to clobber, for the 13th time, the one-third of the population with mortgages ("RBA raises rates, points to further pain ahead", 8/11). There are other means to tackle this problem and spread the obligation to curb inflation across the whole community. Adjustments to the GST and Medicare levy are just two measures that come to mind. Spare us please the recycled platitudes that "we understand your pain". Relying solely on interest rate manipulation is both lazy and unfair. Bryan Francis, Altona
Fairer solution
While I understand the theory that rising interest rates affect demand, which in turn leads to a reduction in prices and consequently a fall in inflation, interest rates alone are not really the panacea to inflation. It's about decreasing demand. Unfortunately, neither side of politics has the political will to address the electorally dangerous path of taxation reform. We need to consider raising the GST. I realise that this initially places immediate pressure on prices, but in time it would reduce demand and ensure those who can afford to spend actually contribute more towards a better functioning and fairer society. David Conolly, Brighton
Turning needs into wants
Interest rate rises do not curb inflation or demand for essential goods and services because people must get what they "need". There is no pressure on providers to hold pricing when they have a captive market. Interest rate rises only reduce spending on discretionary items - "wants" - because people must find the money to meet their needs first.
A new approach is needed, and curbing rampant greed - in its truest sense, meaning to take more than one's fair share - would be a good start. Emma Borghesi, Rye
How to tackle cynicism
Michelle Grattan's insightful piece on the disengagement of the general population from our political system ("Political system in need of repair", 8/11) highlights a trend that has continued from the heady days of Labor's "It's time" campaign in 1972 when there was hope and excitement in the air and politics was widely discussed in pubs and homes.
In his book What Is To Be Done (2020), former Labor minister Barry Jones points out that party membership is less than 30,000 (0.2 per cent of voters) and many of those are unaware they hold party tickets. Party membership is the barometer of good democracy but it does indicate the decline in political engagement in our society.
The question is how do we arrest this cynicism around our democracy? Alienation and distrust of our democratic system will only lead to extremism and disgruntlement. In this regard the teals can teach the major parties a thing or two. They capture the interest of voters by addressing the major issue of our time - climate change. First-preference votes for the major parties (already at record lows) will only further decline unless they respond to the concerns of voters and encourage engagement at all levels of government. Graeme Lechte, Brunswick West
A strange gem
Michelle Grattan raises crucial points. She notes that the major parties are struggling to appeal to voters and asks whether our political system is letting us down. But she says, and most of our politicians, media and academics apparently agree, that our compulsory voting "is a gem in practice". Strangely though, people argue as to whether it is or is not compulsory.
I suggest our system enables powerful political bodies to focus their election strategies on local issues in marginal electorates, ignoring core supporters and party beliefs. A compulsory system requires that obstacles to voting be minimised. Hence, we have many thousands voting weeks before some policies are announced. We have no way of knowing whether a government has a strong mandate because we don't know how many people would have preferred to withhold their vote.
If New Zealand can get a voter turnout of about 80 per cent in a voluntary system, surely Australians could do the same? Michael Doyle, Ashburton
Be thankful
I agree with most of outgoing Liberal MP Matthew Bach's opinions on legalising drugs of dependence ("Lib MP backs drug decriminalisation", 8/11), as long as there are services to assist people. (My addiction is chocolate, but it must be from the Lindt dark range, such as Raspberry Intense.)
However, I am greatly offended by his statement warning Liberals not to listen to "selfish rich geriatrics". I am one of those so-called "selfish geriatrics". Yes I now live a comfortable life with no urgent financial worries. Was this always my situation? No. My generation was thankful to have somewhere to live and to have simple food and clothing supplied by our parents. I grew up in a Housing Commission house. We had no telephone, car or TV. We never visited cafes or restaurants for meals. We never expected to have an overseas holiday. We holidayed at local beaches in a tent. Beside our school uniform, we had maybe two or three other outfits to wear. We were accepting of this life. We were loved, housed, clothed and fed.
As an adult I have always worked. I was a "stay at home" mum but did night-time work a lot of that time. I never had family to assist me with my children. Since retiring, I have participated in numerous volunteering roles, which have given me much pleasure. I believe many of the younger generations have no idea of the sacrifices their parents and grandparents made in their lives. Sacrifices that have enabled the following generations to now have numerous advantages.
Representing our values
In all the coverage regarding our PM's visit to China, I have seen barely a mention of some very important unresolved issues. I am referring to the loss of democracy in Hong Kong, the cultural genocide in Tibet and the incarnation of the Uyghur people. Yes, we must have a working relationship with China, but we must never sell out our values. Barry Lizmore, Ocean Grove
Restraint is reasonable
Your correspondent is critical of the UN calling for "maximum restraint" from Israel (Letters, 8/11), accusing the UN of a lack of impartiality; but the the Israeli PM, Netanyahu, had already foreshadowed the death and destruction that the Israeli Defense Forces were going to unleash on Gaza; it was to this stated intention, and now practice, that the UN was urging "maximum restraint".
No one is suggesting that a superior armed Israel does not have a right to defend itself via an Iron Dome or its new anti-ballistic missile defence system; but an arms race of sorts and periodic escalations in conflict will continue in the region until at least both, if not all, parties acknowledge that the history of human carnage will continue until the governments and people of Israel, Gaza and the West Bank sit down and seriously acknowledge a two-state solution.
This will necessitate international diplomacy and pressure. Brendan O'Farrell, Brunswick
The downside of ceasefire
Your correspondent (Letters, 8/11) complains she has been accused of being pro-terrorist for advocating for a ceasefire in Gaza. While I'm sure she is acting out of concern for Gaza's civilians, the effect of a ceasefire would be to favour Hamas. title: Woodside bullish on gas as oil prices slip:   Fossil fuels
author: Peter Milne
full_text:
Woodside chief executive Meg O'Neill said the company will keep investing in oil and gas, batting down concerns about weaker long-term demand for the fossil fuel amid a global push towards decarbonisation.
O'Neill endured stern questioning at the company's annual investor day yesterday, especially over Woodside's free cash flow outlook, which has slipped as oil prices retreat from their war-fuelled highs.
The Perth-based company flagged a $US7 billion ($11 billion) drop in predicted free cash flow over the next four years. Chief financial officer Graham Tiver attributed the slide to a change to the company's oil price outlook, from about $US85 a barrel to $US70 a barrel.
O'Neill said Woodside's greater scale and global reach from buying BHP's petroleum business and its disciplined approach to new investment would allow it to improve its performance.
Woodside also presented a bullish view of gas demand based on a scenario where global heating caused by fossil fuels to edge up about 2.0 degrees. It also forecast a higher demand for gas even if temperature pushed over 2.5 degrees.
"Supply from gas and oil projects that are operational today and under development will not meet future demand and additional investment in gas and oil is required," O'Neill said.
Both outlooks were based on work released by industry consultant Wood Mackenzie in September that also included a less damaging 1.5-degree scenario it described as "still possible but ... much depends on actions taken this decade." Woodside yesterday did not address the outlook for gas demand in that circumstance.
However, O'Neill added that as Australia's largest oil and gas company Woodside was in a position to withstand the transition from fossil fuels to renewables.
In September, the International Energy Agency reiterated that there was no room for large new fossil projects if global heating was to be limited to 1.5 degrees.
Woodside's next big development was expected to be gas from the Browse fields off the Kimberley coast processed in its existing North West Shelf plant.
"We continue to try to move them forward, but it is a bit of a challenging environment," she said.
Apart from the regulatory approvals, Woodside is also facing delays to Browse from its joint venture partners. The vital agreement to allow Browse gas to be processed through the North West Shelf plant is yet to be finalised despite a non-binding preliminary agreement signed five years ago and regular reporting of positive progress toward a final deal ever since.
O'Neill added that Woodside's $US12 billion Scarborough gas project remained within budget and on track to start in 2026 despite uncertainty over the vulnerability of offshore environmental approvals to legal appeals.
A number of such appeals have stopped drilling and pipeline installation at Woodside rival Santos's Barossa project and halted survey work for the Scarborough project.

title: Hottest year record almost certain to fall
author: Laura Chung
full_text:
This year is "virtually certain" to be the hottest in 125,000 years, as October broke global monthly heat records for the fifth time this year.
Last month smashed the previous record set in 2019 by 0.4 degrees, data released by the Copernicus Climate Change Service found.
"When we combine our data with the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, then we can say that this is the warmest year for the last 125,000 years," Samantha Burgess, deputy director of the Copernicus Climate Change Service told Reuters. An agency statement added that this meant 2023 was "virtually certain" to be the hottest on record.
Meanwhile, the average surface air temperature was 15.3 degrees, 0.85 degrees above the 1991-2020 average for October.
The first 10 months of this year have recorded the highest global mean temperature at 1.43 degrees above the 1850-1900 pre-industrial average, and 0.1 degree hotter than the 10-month average for 2016 - the warmest year on record.
That year, the Great Barrier Reef experienced some of its worst coral bleaching as global temperatures soared during an El Nino event, which makes the weather hotter and drier.
The data comes just weeks before COP28, the annual United Nations climate meeting, where governments will discuss how to limit and prepare for future climate change, as well as what progress has been made to reduce emissions since the 2015 Paris Agreement. Already this year, June, July, August and September have been the hottest-ever consecutive months globally.
Melbourne University climate scientist Dr Andrew King said while El Nino was contributing to the heat, it didn't explain the massive temperature anomalies. "Human-caused climate change, due to our ongoing high greenhouse gas emissions, is the main reason we're seeing record high global temperatures," he said.
"For Australia, October was dry but not especially hot. With the continuing El Nino we should be prepared for drought development and a higher chance of extreme heat events in the coming months."
Monash University associate professor in the School of Earth, Atmosphere and Environment Dr Ailie Gallant described the data as "mind-boggling", and warned warming would continue without aggressive action to limit greenhouse gases.
"[The figures] are just insane," she said. "This is something as climate scientists, we look at our computer screens and think, 'Yes this will happen one day.' But that day is now."
Emeritus Professor Ian Lowe from Griffith University, the former president of the Australian Conservation Foundation, said he was disappointed by the lack of mitigation measures implemented.
"While Australian people have voted with their wallets and embraced solar electricity, we still don't have policies to clean up our transport, agriculture and industry," he said.

title: Glencore's $10.6b plan to shake up the mining world:   Comment
author: Stephen Bartholomeusz
full_text:
Three years ago, former Glencore chief executive Ivan Glasenberg approached Canada's Teck Resources with a typically bold and opportunistic proposal: Let's merge the companies and spin off their combined coal businesses.
His plan was rejected at the time, but now his successor Gary Nagle has pulled off half the deal Glasenberg envisaged.
This week, Glencore and Teck announced a $US6.9 billion ($10.6 billion) agreement under which Glencore will acquire the Canadian company's metallurgical coal operations and merge them with its own, industry-leading energy coal business.
Japan's Nippon Steel and South Korea's Posco, which have minority stakes in Teck coal mines, will roll their interests into shareholdings in Teck's Elk Valley Resources, enabling Glencore to emerge with a 77 per cent stake in a coal business with an enterprise value of about $US9 billion. Nippon Steel will own 21 per cent, and Posco will have 3 per cent.
Glencore will then merge Teck's coal assets with its own, with plans to spin off the combined businesses as a new listed company within two years of implementation of the deal, which is expected in the third quarter of next year.
Nagle had revived the Glasenberg proposal rebuffed by Teck in 2020 earlier this year, when he scuppered the Canadian company's own plans to separate its coal and base metal businesses.
Teck's plans were complicated by the fact that its copper and zinc operations, among the fastest growing in their sector, are immature and reliant on the cash flows from its coal mines for funding.
To solve this, the company proposed, peculiarly, that even after demerging the businesses it would receive royalties from the coal operations for the next six years; royalties equivalent to about 90 per cent of the assets' free cash flows.
Nagle proposed a cleaner $US23 billion takeover offer, initially all-scrip and subsequently with a $US8.2 billion cash component, followed by a demerger of the combined coal operations that would have resulted in the ongoing Glencore emerging as the biggest pure play in future-facing metals, combining Teck's copper and zinc assets with its own copper, nickel, zinc and cobalt assets.
With Teck's founding family holding a majority of its super-voting "A-class" shares, Nagle, like his predecessor, wasn't able to convince his target of the merits of his proposal - but he did succeed in killing off Teck's own planned demerger, which eventually led to the deal announced this week.
That was only half the original Glasenberg vision, but leaves open the possibility that Nagle could eventually complete what he set out to do in April.
There is a standstill agreement between Glencore and Teck that prohibits Glencore from acquiring shares in the Canadian company for two years from completion of the coal deal which, if the deal timetable is met, would be the third quarter of 2026.
Coincidentally, or more likely conveniently, the end of that standstill agreement would occur just as the two-year integration of the two coal units and the deleveraging of Glencore that Nagle envisages (he wants to halve net debt from $US10 billion to $US5 billion) would be completed and the combined coal business demerged and separately listed.
The standstill would cease if a third party was to bid for Teck. But if no one targeting Teck's base metal assets emerges, it's not going to surprise anyone if Nagle has another crack at acquiring arguably the largest and most attractive suite of base metals assets not owned by the major resource companies and creating a very big pure play in the metals vital to meet global carbon emissions targets.
The issue of carbon emissions is a major influence over Glencore's strategy, as it has been for some years.
Glasenberg, before he retired in 2021, committed Glencore to reducing its carbon emissions, and those of its customers, to net-zero by 2050.
That might have appeared odd, coming from a company that emits more carbon than many mid-sized countries, but it demonstrated typically clever thinking.
As the world's largest seaborne energy coal producer and marketer, Glencore can finesse the relationship between the volumes of coal it produces - about 110 million tonnes a year - and the prices it receives for its own coal and those of third-party producers that it markets.
By allowing its reserves to deplete and running them to maximise the cash they generate in an environment where new mines face increasing obstacles, Glencore increases its influence over the market and the pricing of its coal. It is prepared to trade volume for value as the reserves of its existing mines, and those that it acquires, deplete.
Adding Teck's mines to its existing operations not only increases their value and life - metallurgical coal, used in steelmaking, trades at materially more than twice the price of energy coal and is essential to the manufacturing of the steel for wind turbines and solar panels - but increases Glencore's influence over the market.
Glencore has come under pressure from activist investors over its near-dominant position in energy coal, a position it has strengthened by hoovering up the coal assets that other miners like Rio Tinto and BHP have offloaded to burnish their green credentials.
Under Glasenberg, Glencore was built on its coal assets, which were the major appeal in its $US90 billion reverse takeover of Xstrata in 2013. Coal is Glencore's biggest profit centre and cash generator, but it's also probably the reason the company trades at far lower price-earnings multiples than other big resource companies like BHP, Rio and Anglo American.
Acquiring Teck's coal assets, combining them with its own and then spinning off the enlarged business as a standalone coal company pursuing the same strategy of depletion and focus on cash generation should unlock considerable value.
It should also enable Glencore to present itself as a clean pure play on future-facing metals and give its shareholders (including Glasenberg, who owns nearly 10 per cent of Glencore) the choice of whether to sell or hold their exposures to coal.
It would, however, also leave Glencore undersized relative to its always oversized ambitions. That's why it is hard to see Nagle simply abandoning his original plan of bulking up both his base metals and coal businesses to set Glencore up for their demerger.
Teck, of course, isn't the only potential target to realise that plan, but it is the best available fit to complete the strategy that Glasenberg envisaged and Nagle is well on his way to executing.

title: The threat to Australia's 'flying koala'
author: Mike Foley
full_text:
Greater gliders were once a common feature of our forests, but experts say only urgent action can save them, writes Mike Foley.
It's 10 minutes after sunset in a misty forest in south-eastern Australia, and one of the most threatened mammals in the world is peering down from its perch in a centuries-old gum tree at the gaggle of people below.
Greater gliders - the world's largest gliding marsupial - are the flying koalas that most people haven't heard of and fewer have seen.
The fluffy forest dweller with satellite-dish ears can glide through the air for up to 100 metres, zooming from tree to tree in a furry wingsuit that stretches between its front and back legs.
Nature's unlikely design for greater gliders could have been lifted from a children's book, but unfortunately for animal lovers, they're much harder to spot than koalas.
They come with all manner of markings - their fur coats range from all-black to all-white and everything in between. Gliders weigh up to 1.6 kilograms, less than half the weight of a small female koala, and live their entire lives high in the canopy, hidden in their homes until dark.
That's why a photographer, two scientists and a reporter stood shivering on a cold November night beneath a tree in Tallaganda National Park, east of Canberra, staring up into the darkness in the hope of catching a glimpse of the elusive marsupial.
It was the same tree where, two days earlier, conservation biologist Ana Gracanin spotted a greater glider slipping inside the stump of a fallen branch 20 metres up.
"These old trees form hollows, and inside is where we find greater gliders and dozens of other marsupial species," says Gracanin, a post-doctoral research fellow at the Australian National University.
"They generally try to avoid gliding. They move through the canopy with their amazing paws that allow them to go on branches that are only 5 millimetres thick to climb through the canopy.
"When there is no canopy for them, or they are spooked by a predator, they will launch off the tree and glide."
Through the gloom, a little blaze of white appears within a jet-black hole in the tree branch and, moments later, torches click on to reveal a greater glider emerging from the tree hollow.
This glider looks like it barely registers the intruders below. A side effect of its diet of eucalyptus leaves, which are low in nutrition and high in toxins, is a slow metabolism and dozy disposition - much like koalas.
Tallaganda National Park is one of the last remaining strongholds for gliders, which were once common in forests from the tip of Cape York down the eastern seaboard into Central Victoria.
But greater gliders - scientific name petauroides volans - are now so rare that the species was last year listed as endangered - a classification the federal government gives to animals at imminent risk of extinction in the wild.
ANU ecologist Dr Kara Youngentob has spent two decades studying gliders, which she says are now "functionally extinct" in many locations, meaning the population is not robust enough to sustain itself into the future.
"They've gone extinct from regions where there used to be lots of them," Youngentob says.
The species' overall population has fallen 80 per cent in the past two decades.
"When I first started working with gliders 20 years ago, they were very common. They were on a decline, but they weren't hard to find. But now, places that I work, there are no gliders there any more," Youngentob says.
When top forest predator the powerful owl takes up a roost in a new patch of forest, it kills all the gliders in surrounding trees before moving on to a new feeding ground. But experts say logging is the biggest threat to the survival of the species, followed by habitat loss due to urban development and global warming.
Global warming is making the weather hotter more frequently, which is more bad news for gliders. Hotter, drier weather is spurring bigger, hotter bushfires that destroy gliders' habitat. It's also putting them off their dinner. "These guys get all their water from their food, and they lose their appetite when they get too hot. It doesn't take long for them to die outright," Youngentob says.
Next door to Tallaganda National Park, in which timber harvesting is banned, Tallaganda State Forest is an active logging area.
NSW's Environment Protection Authority earlier this year shut down logging in the state forest after it ruled state forestry workers had failed to set up the required 50-metre exclusion zones around trees where gliders were living.
Conservation groups have criticised NSW Forestry Corporation for searching for gliders only during the day when they are almost impossible to find, while the logging corporation argues there is no requirement to search for them at night.
A NSW Forestry Corp survey of an area in Tallaganda in October identified just one tree where gliders had made a den. But the Environment Protection Authority issued a stop-work order after it identified 20 habitat trees.
While the Commonwealth has sweeping powers to protect native species, the Albanese government is already a year overdue on its promise to reform national environment laws under the Environment Protection and Biodiversity Conservation Act.
Experts warn far greater protections are urgently needed because current safeguards are failing to slow the pace of native wildlife losses.
Australia is a global hotspot for wildlife extinctions. Since colonisation, Australia has lost 34 mammals, which is about the same number as the rest of the world combined over the past 200 years.
Federal Environment Minister Tanya Plibersek has pledged to lodge her reforms in parliament sometime next year, promising to rectify one of the most controversial aspects of the current laws - regional forestry agreements. These agreements, struck between federal and state governments, in effect exempt native forest logging from national environment laws, including threatened species protections.
"Our government has already announced that for the first time in Australian history, regional forest agreements will have to comply with national environmental law," Plibersek says.
Professor David Lindenmayer, an eminent conservation scientist and Biodiversity Council member, is working in Booderee National Park, in Jervis Bay on NSW's South Coast, in a bid to reintroduce gliders there.
They disappeared from the largely untouched landscape in 2007, a troubling development that he puts down to a combination of factors.
"It's hard to find the cause other than it was around about that time that there was a lot of urban development at the base of the peninsula, which is Jervis Bay. Then we had big fires in 2003 and we've had a series of very, very, very hot summers with very high overnight temperatures," Lindenmayer says. Youngentob and Lindenmayer are focused on finding the best micro-climates in the park, with cooler conditions, that may offer the best chance to any reintroduced gliders.
"We're going to give it the best shot that we can with the best possible science," Lindenmayer says.
A spokesperson for Forestry Corp says it believes it has been complying with regulations and implementing the same regime for the past five years. The corporation is seeking clarification from the EPA about its stop-work order.
